title: Fix desktop builds on Windows for apps with "use server" actions
text:
Fix desktop builds on Windows for apps with "use server" actions
Running `rustybuns build desktop` **on** Windows failed for any app with `"use server"` actions. This is why the `windows-x64` job of the motion-midi workflow has failed since 0.1.5, when that workflow first ran.

On Windows, `join()` gives `D:\a\...\bounce.ts`, while Vite gives `D:/a/.../bounce.ts`. title: Cost guards: billable-resource report on plan/deploy, opt-in for large Hetzner boxes
text:
Cost guards: billable-resource report on plan/deploy, opt-in for large Hetzner boxes
Guards against surprise Cloudflare and Hetzner bills, at the framework level so every app gets them.

**CLI** (`packages/cli/src/costs.ts`)
- `rustybuns plan` / `deploy` print the stack's billable resources first, marked **fixed** (hourly, Hetzner server + Volume) or **usage** (Worker, Durable Objects, D1, KV, R2).
- Hard stop: a Hetzner `serverType` past the small shared tiers (`ccx*`, tier 3+ like `cpx31`, or an unrecognised name) is refused unless `targets.box.allowLargeServer: true`. `--yes` does not skip it.
- After a box deploy: a reminder that it bills hourly until `rustybuns destroy`.

title: park-hide-seek: live weather and the park's real time of day
text:
park-hide-seek: live weather and the park's real time of day
Follow-up to #20.

At the moment the lobby picks day, dusk or night by hand. Instead, pull the park's actual conditions when a round starts and play in them.

**Source:** [Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com). It needs no API key and is free for non-commercial use, which fits an example app. Checked from Yosemite: `/v1/forecast?latitude=..&longitude=..&current=temperature_2m,weather_code,cloud_cover,wind_speed_10m,precipitation,is_day&timezone=auto` answers with all of those fields.

**Ideas**
- **Time of day:** use `is_day` and the local time to choose between day, dusk and night. Keep a manual override in the lobby.
- **Rain:** particles, and it hides footsteps (rangers hear less).
- **Fog:** shorter sight ranges, using `SIGHT.range` in `src/hunt/sim.ts`.
- **Wind:** bushes sway, and rustles from call-outs are harder to place (more jitter).
- **Clouds:** darker nights with no moon.

**Notes**
- The host fetches the weather once per round and sends it in the view, so every player gets the same conditions. On a LAN the guests never call the API themselves.
- If the fetch fails or the machine is offline, fall back to the lobby setting.
- Gameplay effects belong in the shared sim, so 
park-hide-seek: live weather and the park's real time of day
Closes #21.

A round now plays in the park's real conditions by default. The lobby still has Day, Dusk and Night as a manual override.

**How it works**
- `src/weather.ts` calls Open-Meteo for the zone's centre using the fields from the issue, plus `daily=sunrise,sunset`. It works out the time of day from the park's local time: dusk is roughly 35–40 min either side of sunset and sunrise, with `is_day` as the fallback. It turns the WMO weather code, wind, cloud and precipitation into a `Sky` (`tod`, `fog`, `rain`, `wind`, `overcast`, `snow`). Each reading is cached for 10 min, and the request g

title: apps/agent-office: Agent Office on Bun, as one self-contained binary
text:
apps/agent-office: Agent Office on Bun, as one self-contained binary
[Agent Office](https://github.com/AgentSystemLabs/agent-office) (MIT) is the cartoon 3D office some of Rusty Buns was built in. This example turns it into **one file** for macOS and Linux. The machine running it needs no Node, no `npm ci` and nothing compiled. Nothing upstream is forked.

```sh
cd apps/agent-office
bun run office              # fetch the latest release, Bun-ify it, open the office
bun run desktop:build       # dist/agent-office-<os>-<arch>, ~79-98 MB
bun run desktop:build:all   # + darwin-x64, linux-x64, linux-arm64

title: native: build Linux crates in Docker when the target isn't this machine (Hetzner, live)
text:
native: build Linux crates in Docker when the target isn't this machine (Hetzner, live)
## What

Rust `native/` crates for a Hetzner box (or a Linux desktop target) no longer need a Linux machine. cdylibs don't cross-compile, so when the target isn't this machine, `build box` / `build desktop` build them in Docker: `rust:<your rustc>-slim-bookworm` for `linux/amd64` (or `linux/arm64` on `cax`), with its own target dir and a cached cargo registry volume. The output goes to `native/dist/<crate>/linux-<arch>/` and is embedded as usual. Bookworm's glibc (2.36) is older than Ubuntu 24.04's (2.39), so the library loads on the server. Without Docker running, the build says to start it.

Adds an opt-in `experimental.wheel` to `rustybuns.config.ts`, which decides who can unlock a stack's `secret` bindings.

title: codeSplitters: branches and line-by-line merges for agents
text:
codeSplitters: merge and conflict flow for agent branches
The contest brief asks for multiple agents working on one codebase with merges and review. codeSplitters has per-line ops with conflicts (409 and skipped ops), but no branches, pull requests, merge or review step. Design the smallest flow that lets an agent work on its own branch and a human or another agent merge it. Decide whether it builds on Artifacts git branches or the line-op log.
codeSplitters: branches and line-by-line merges for agents
Closes #110.

**Decision: built on the line-op log, not Artifacts git branches.** On a branch, each file is a copy of that file's Durable Object, forked from main with the same line ids and revs. That means a merge can match lines by id instead of diffing text, blame and live sync work the same on a branch, and git hears about the work only when main is catalogued (committed).

### The flow
- `POST /api/repos/:o/:r/branches {name}`: anyone with write access opens a branch.
- Edit with `?branch=name` on the usual `/do/*` routes (sockets too), or `POST /files {path, content, branch}` for a new f

`src/sync.ts` builds an LCS table of base lines times next lines. Over `MAX_CELLS` (4,000,000) it stops matching, so every line counts as changed. That replaces the whole file and loses the original author of each line in blame. Replace the LCS with a linear diff (Myers or patience) so large files keep their ids.
codeSplitters: agent edits skipped when a human changed the same line
When a line changes while an agent works, the agent's op on that line is dropped and reported as skipped. Nothing re-runs the agent or asks for a merge, so the agent's change to that line is lost. Decide the policy: re-run the agent on the new text, show the conflict to the human, or keep the human's version. Right now the CLI only prints the skipped count.

title: codeSplitters: hosted agents run in a Cloudflare container
text:
codeSplitters: hosted agents need a sandbox; the runner is desktop-only
`agent.ts` spawns the CLI on the machine running it, so it works from the desktop app or a laptop. It cannot run on the Cloudflare deploy, where there is no CLI and no filesystem. Hosted agents need Cloudflare Containers (announced in Birthday Week) with each CLI installed and its login set as a secret. Also needed for agents to run tests or builds.

The agent runner only worked where the CLI was installed. On Cloudflare there is no CLI and no filesystem, so now the app can run the agent in a container.

text:

`rustybuns plan`/`deploy` doesn't pass the config's names to Alchemy. The Worker gets no `name` (the config's `name`), and D1 gets no `databaseName`, nor R2 a `bucketName` (`packages/cli/src/gen/alchemy.ts`). So Alchemy makes `<app>-<id>-<stage>-<random>` names, and a stack whose local state is gone plans to **create** everything again.

**What happened:** codesplitters is live as Worker `codesplitters` with D1 `codesplitters-db`, made with wrangler. `rustybuns plan` wanted to create a new Worker and a new, empty database beside them, so we deployed with `wrangler deploy` instead. The same thing already left four orphaned `druids-curse-...-DB-live-ryanquinn-*` databases (see the cleanup issue).

**Fix:**
- Emit the explicit names: Worker `name: cfg.name`, D1 `name: databaseName`, R2 `name: bucketName`. Alchemy's D1 already adopts a database by name when creating it hits "already exists".
- Pass `--adopt` when nothing's in state.
- Careful with live Alchemy-managed apps (hippo, druids): a name change replaces resources there, so do it per app or behind a flag.

A Worker made with wrangler has no Alchemy tags, so Alchemy treats it as someone else's and refuses it unless told to take it over. title: rustybuns deploy: share Alchemy state across worktrees so it outlives them (#171)
text:
rustybuns deploy: keep Alchemy state somewhere that outlives the worktree
Follow-up to #140 / #169.

The generated stack uses `Alchemy.localState()`, so state lives in `.alchemy/` inside the worktree. Deleting a worktree (e.g. when an office worker is sent home) loses it. The next plan then has to rediscover everything.

`targets.edge.adopt` (#169) means a lost state no longer creates duplicates for D1, R2 and the Worker. Other resources still do (KV namespaces, which have no name in the config; Railway/Hetzner resources). Minted secrets (`experimental.wheel "agent"`) also live in that state and come back different.

Options to weigh:
- a state dir outside the worktree, e.g. keyed by repo + app + stage under `~/.alchemy` or the main checkout;
- Alchemy's HTTP or Postgres state store (`src/State/HttpStateStore.ts`, `PostgresState.ts` in beta.77);
- a config key to choose, defaulting to the shared local dir.

Watch out for two worktrees deploying the same stage at once.

title: hippo-tycoon: keep the Rust sim resident (bots in Rust + compact snapshot), default in solo/couch
text:
hippo-tycoon: keep the Rust sim's state resident (port bots + snapshot) to make it a win in play
Follow-up from #33. The Rust twin of `step()` (`rust/crates/hippo_sim`) is ~1.6x faster than the TypeScript step when its state stays inside the module, but in the game every tick copies `State` in and out because bots (`src/sim/bots.ts`), `Match.snapshot()` and the room all read the TypeScript `State`. With that copy it is slower than TypeScript (~780k vs ~1,350k ticks/s, `bun bench/sim.ts`), so it is opt-in (`?sim=rust`) and the room DO / desktop world stay on TypeScript.

To make it the default: port `bots.ts` to the crate (it uses `Math.hypot`; switch to `len()` from `src/sim/trig.ts` first), export a compact snapshot from Rust instead of the whole state, and load the wasm in the Worker / desktop world. Only worth it if the sim's cost ever matters (today both engines are far under 0.01% of a 30 Hz frame).

title: Cron Triggers in Rusty Buns + codeSplitters dependency doctor
text:
codeSplitters: dependency doctor — scheduled dependency updates that build, test and fix themselves
On a schedule the user can tune, find outdated packages, try each update on a branch, build and test it in a throwaway Rusty Buns sandbox, and have an agent fix whatever breaks. People only see updates that are ready to merge.

**Flow**
1. Cron fires (a Workers Cron Trigger on the edge; Rusty Buns has no cron yet, so the desktop twin needs one).
2. Read the lockfile and check the registry for updates.
3. Open one line branch per update, or per group.
4. Build and test in the sandbox container, then tear it down.
5. If it breaks: an agent reads the changelog and the repo's line history (who calls this API, since when) and patches the affected code as line ops on the branch, blamed on `agent-deps`.
6. Green → a merge that's ready for review. Still red after N tries → one short report on why.

**Settings to keep updates from piling up**
- How often it runs, and whether to group updates (all patches in one branch, say).
- Policy by level: auto-merge patches, review minors, have the agent attempt majors.
- Minimum release age (wait N days after a version is published). This also guards against compromised packages.
- Ignore or snooze packages that release too often.

text:
codeSplitters: private lines inside a public repo
Privacy is per repo today. A range of lines can be shared out of a private repo, but you can't mark single lines private inside a public one.

The hard part is git: a public repo's remote serves whole files, so private lines would have to be redacted from what is pushed (like sealed lines or secrets), and blame, search, shares, playlists and the game walls must all respect it. Design it before building:

- Who sees a private line (owner, crew, named people)?
- What do others see: a placeholder line, or nothing?
- What does the git remote get, and how does a clone by the crew get the real text?

Follow-up to #197 / #241. On Cloudflare, a scheduled doctor run tests in AGENT_SANDBOX containers inside the cron's `waitUntil`. Each try is a cold container plus `bun install` plus tests. A repo with many updates that break together gets tried together, then one by one, then together again, and that could run past the cron's wall-clock limit. Follow-up to the merge change that follows moved lines.

When main moves a line and the branch inserted new lines right after it, the merge follows the move for edits to that line, but the branch's new lines are still placed at the line's old position, not under it in its new one. Moves are also only recognised when the moved text is unambiguous (one deleted copy, one inserted copy, not blank); a block of repeated lines (e.g. several `}`) moved together isn't matched as a move.

Possible fix: carry the anchor through moved lines, and match moved blocks as contiguous runs rather than single lines.

Closes #249.

**Cause:** this wasn't load making edits race the commit. All edits finish before the commit runs. The renamer changed `foo` → `total` one line at a time. If the linter read the file after `var total = 0` but before `foo = foo + n` was renamed, it saw no reassignment of `total` and chose `const`. Its `ifRev` check still passed because nothing changed between its read and its write. The result was `const total = 0`, and the test's `let total = 0` check failed.

**Fix:** `agents.ts`: `pick` now returns `ops: Op[]`, and the renamer sends every rename as one all-or-nothing batch, so

title: codeSplitters limits: a "queue" on-fail action for digs
text:
codeSplitters limits: a "queue" on-fail action for slow, costly jobs (Cloudflare Queues)
Follow-up from #262, which adds the rate-limits page and the reject / log / flag on-fail actions.

A fourth action, **queue**, would hold an over-the-cap request and run it later instead of rejecting it. The user would see "you're 3rd in line" instead of a 429. A queue consumer with `max_batch_size` and `max_concurrency` would control the pace.

It only fits slow, costly jobs: digs (Artifacts imports), preview deploys and dependency-doctor runs. Line edits are pinned to the file's rev, so a queued edit would come back as a conflict. Sign-ins should stay rejected.

Needs a decision first:
- A new billed resource: a Cloudflare Queues binding (Workers Paid; pennies at this volume, but it's new spend).
- Those routes answer synchronously today, so they'd need to become jobs with a status the page polls.
- Hosted agent runs are already admin-only, and admins are never limited, so queueing doesn't help them yet.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
codeSplitters limits: a "queue" on-fail action for digs
Closes #268.

A dig over its cap can now **queue** instead of getting a 429. The request answers 202 with the caller's place in line and about when it will run (the page shows "you're 2nd in line, about 12 minutes"). It waits in a new D1 table, `limit_jobs`. Once the caller's window has room, it's replayed as them. That happens when the page polls `GET /api/jobs/:id`, or on the existing five-minute cron for callers who closed the tab. The replay takes one of the window's slots and isn't counted again.

title: rustybuns: crates opt out of desktop; hippo-tycoon's wasm crates move to native/ (#164)
text:
The Rust dilemma: native crates, cross builds and FFI safety
All the open issues about the Rust side of RustyBuns (the `native/` crates, how they're built, and how binaries load them), in one place. Each one stays open with its full details; this issue just ties them together.

## Safety: native code you can trip over
- [x] #154 **auto-rig panics on a crafted mesh.** `native/crates/auto_rig` uses face indices without checking them against the vertex count; a bad index panics across FFI and aborts the desktop app. Fix: bounds-check, or return an error instead of panicking.
- [x] #150 **Compiled binaries load Rust libraries from the current folder first.** `packages/native/src/index.ts` tries `process.cwd()/native/dist/...` before the embedded copy, so a planted library in the working folder gets `dlopen`ed. Fix: in compiled binaries, only load the embedded copy or an explicit `opts.dir`.

## Build: what gets compiled and shipped
- [x] #114 **Linux cross targets build every crate in Docker,** even wasm-only ones that shouldn't be embedded, unless the app sets `desktop.native: false`. Fix: let each crate say whether it ships to desktop (e.g. `[package.metadata.rustybuns] desktop = false`), or document `native: false` more prominently.
- [x] #11
rustybuns: Linux cross targets build native/ in Docker even when nothing would be embedded
Follow-up from #36 / #111.

#111 narrowed the macOS/Windows cross refusal: it now fires only when a crate would be embedded (named in \`desktop.native\`, or built into \`native/dist\`). Linux cross targets weren't changed. When \`native/Cargo.toml\` exists and \`desktop.native\` isn't \`false\`, \`build desktop --target linux-*\` off-Linux still:
- requires Docker, and
- builds **every** crate in \`native/crates\` as a Linux cdylib, then embeds it.

A wasm-only crate therefore gets built for Linux in Docker and shipped in the binary for nothing, unless the app sets \`desktop.native: false\`. I kept this behaviour on purpose: FFI apps that don't set \`desktop.native\` (fm-daw, motion-midi) and have no \`native/dist\` yet rely on the Docker build.

Possible fix: decide what ships from the crate itself rather than from \`native/dist\`. For example, skip crates with a \`wasm32\`-only marker, or with a \`[package.metadata.rustybuns] desktop = false\`. Then the Docker build and the staging both use that list. The other option is to keep \`native: false\` as the answer and document it more prominently.

text:

Found while testing #284 on the live Worker (codesplitters.notryanquinn.workers.dev), 2026-10-10 around 11:00 to 11:15 UTC.

Some requests never answer. The client gives up and `wrangler tail` logs them as `canceled`, with no logs or exceptions:

- `POST /api/auth/sign-in/email` for an **existing** email account hangs every time (5 out of 5 tries, cut off at 15s each). The same call with an unknown email answers `401 INVALID_EMAIL_OR_PASSWORD` in about 0.3s.
- `POST /api/auth/sign-up/email` sometimes hangs (60s and 40s with no answer) and sometimes answers in under a second. The hung ones never wrote a `user` row.
- Later, `GET /api/admin/limits` (signed in as admin) hung too (cut off at 10s and 15s). `/api/session`, `/api/levels` and `/api/jobs` in the same tab answered in about 200ms.

D1 isn't slow: direct queries take under 1ms, and the tables are small (19 `limit_hits` rows, 4 sessions).

Guesses, not checked: password hashing (scrypt in better-auth 1.7.7) never finishing on Workers, or a pending promise held at isolate level (the `authFor` WeakMap, or the module-level `cache` in `limits.ts`) that later requests wait on.

Loose ends from #244:

Found while checking fresh start on real Cloudflare Artifacts (#314).

Cloudflare's import (`ARTIFACTS.import`, `POST …/repos/:name/import`) refuses a repo whose shallow clone is over 40 MB:

```
413 {"code":10402,"message":"Repository at \"https://github.com/alchemy-run/alchemy.git\" exceeded the 40MB import limit. Current depth is 1. Try a smaller value to fetch less history."}
```

Alchemy's tip is about 44 MB packed (19,857 files), so this is already depth 1. Both places that import do it at depth 1 and can't go smaller:

The [Artifacts limits page](https://developers.cloudflare.com/artifacts/platform/limits/) lists 1 GB of storage per repository and 32 MB per file or blob.

text:
rustybuns deploy: refuse a live deploy from a branch behind main, or one that deletes a stateful resource
Found while checking #348 on live codeSplitters.

Agents deploy codeSplitters from their own worktrees (shared Alchemy state). While I was checking #348, #353 merged and was deployed from another worktree, adding the R2 bucket `LEVEL_CHUNKS`. My next deploy came from a branch cut before #353, so its plan said `[LEVEL_CHUNKS] delete`. I chained plan and deploy without reading the plan, and the deploy deleted the bucket and rolled the Worker back to before #353/#354 for about 80 seconds. I rebased and redeployed straight away. The bucket was empty (no level had `store = 'r2'` yet), so nothing was lost.

**Ask:** `rustybuns deploy` (on a target with `adopt: true`, i.e. a live site) should refuse when HEAD doesn't contain `origin/main`, unless `--force` is passed. It should also refuse a plan that deletes a stateful resource (R2, D1, KV, DO class) without an explicit flag.

rustybuns deploy: refuse a live deploy from a branch behind main, or one that deletes stateful resources (#363)
Closes #363.

title: cli: plan and deploy build the Worker before Alchemy hashes its bundle (#362)
text:
rustybuns deploy ships the previous build's bundle
Found while checking #348 on live codeSplitters.

`rustybuns deploy` ships the bundle from the **previous** build. Alchemy works out the Worker's diff (and uploads `dist/worker/worker.js`) from what's on disk before the `Build` command runs, so the first deploy after a code change only rebuilds:

```
[Build] update
Done: 1 succeeded (145ms)      <- Worker not updated
```

and only the next deploy ships it (`[Worker] update`). The same goes for `plan`, which said "no Worker change" for a code-only change.

Worse, a deploy that changes bindings uploads the old bundle along with the new bindings. In #348 a deploy added the `LEVEL_CHUNKS` binding but shipped a bundle built before the code that uses it.

**To fix:** make the Worker depend on the Build's output (so it hashes after the build), or have `rustybuns deploy` run the build before handing over to Alchemy.

For now, deploy twice, or run `bun run build.ts` before deploying.

Follow-up from #248 (PR #346). `rustybuns build box` cross-builds `native/` crates in Docker when the box's arch isn't the build machine's (REFERENCE.md, "Rust crates build in Docker off Linux"). The hosted deploy container (`deploy-sandbox/Dockerfile`) has no Docker, so a Railway or Hetzner box with such crates fails to build from the site. text:
rustybuns init: build command skips prebuild steps, misses some vite aliases and non-default configs
Found porting 5 webpack apps to Vite and running init on them (see #400).

- **Prebuild steps skipped.** For a static app, init writes `vite build --outDir dist/web` and ignores the app's own build script. CyberChef must run its config generators (and a postinstall patch) before bundling, so a fresh clone fails. Init could keep the build script's steps before `vite build` (as `inferWorkerBuild` does for Workers), or honor a `prebuild` script.
- **Alias not read.** `alias: { "@": fileURLToPath(new URL("./src", import.meta.url)) }` (Yacht) gives `aliases: {}`. `inferVite` only reads `resolve(…, "x")` and string forms.
- **Non-default vite config.** An app whose build config isn't `vite.config.*` (e.g. `vite.app.config.ts` beside a vitest one) gets a build that uses the wrong config, and `root` is read from the wrong file.

title: codeSplitters mirrors: rewrite detection works right after Push the crew's copy (#410)
text:
codeSplitters mirrors: rewrite detection can miss on the crew's copy right after Push the crew's copy
Rewrite detection (#398) checks whether `upstream_commit`, the last commit both sides agreed on, is still in upstream's history. The crew's bare repo was forked from the repo's own git when the first private line was made. If the repo's own git synced newer upstream commits after that, `upstream_commit` may not be in the crew's repo.

When the owner first turns on **Push the crew's copy**, the check is then skipped (`cat-file -e` fails). A force-push in that window falls back to `merge-tree` finding no common history. That still lands on **rewritten**, but **Re-base** can't tell which commits are this copy's own, so only **Take upstream's** works.

Fix idea: when turning on pushCrew, fetch `upstream_commit` from the repo's own git into the crew's repo.

title: codeSplitters mirrors: a force-pushed upstream is fetched only back to the agreed commit (#409)
text:
codeSplitters mirrors: a force-pushed upstream is fetched in full
Mirrors clone shallow (`--depth 1`), but each sync's `git fetch` (src/mirror.ts, step 1) has no depth. When upstream force-pushes a rewritten history, nothing in it is known locally, so the fetch pulls the whole new history. On a big repo that's slow and large on disk, just to reach the **rewritten** state.

Fix idea: fetch with `--depth` (or `--shallow-exclude`) when the new tip doesn't descend from `upstream_commit`. Re-base only needs upstream's new tip.

title: codeSplitters tests: settle() fails loudly when a hosted deploy is still running (#287)
text:
codeSplitters: flaky test "needs a key; then runs in its own container..." (destroy lands after the run reads as done)
Failed once in ~5 full \`bun test\` runs of apps/codesplitters (test/deploy-hosted.test.ts, "a hosted deploy"), in 4.4s, so not a timeout:

```
178 |     expect(seen.destroyed).toBe(1);
Expected: 1
Received: 0

Seen while testing #403 live (create-vue app, static/assets-only Worker, stage `live403`, since destroyed).

title: agent-office: GitHub boards hear webhooks through gh webhook forward (#466)
text:
agent-office: push GitHub changes to the boards (webhooks) instead of watching
The live boards (apps/agent-office/live/github.ts) catch a worker's own \`gh\` writes and pushes immediately. For everything else, a busy floor checks GitHub every 10s with free conditional requests. What's still missing is a real push from GitHub, which would also cover idle floors and changes made on github.com within about 1s.

Options:
- **\`gh webhook forward\`**: GitHub relays the repo's webhooks to localhost over a websocket, so no public URL is needed. Catches: it's a beta gh extension, it needs repo admin, and only one forwarder per repo can run at a time.
- **Cloudflare Worker + Durable Object**: the Worker receives the repo webhook and verifies its secret, and the office holds an outbound websocket to the DO. This needs a deploy and a secret (via varlock), on the smallest plan.

On an event, call the floor's \`refreshIssues\` / \`refreshPulls\`, or apply the payload directly. Do this only if the 10s watch turns out not to be enough.

text:
codeSplitters checks: one panel for our runs and GitHub Actions, and a merge gate
Part of dogfooding: codeSplitters hosts codeSplitters (and RustyBuns), with GitHub as the backup. This issue ties together the build/CI runner (#463) and the desktop as the primary git store (#464).

## What

One place to see whether a change is good, wherever it ran. A push to GitHub still triggers the existing pipeline (`typecheck.yml`, `apps.yml`), and codeSplitters can also build, test and gate on its own runs.

## Scope

1. **Triggers.** A commit to main, an update to an open branch, and a branch pushed upstream each start check runs (#463). A setting per repo chooses where they run: `here`, `github` or `both`. RustyBuns starts with `both`, to compare the two.
2. **GitHub results come back in.** After a branch or commit goes up through the mirror, poll the GitHub check-runs / commit-status API for that sha with the existing token, and record each job as a `runner: "github"` check run. Actions results then show next to codeSplitters' own.
3. **Our results go out.** Optionally post codeSplitters' own check runs to GitHub as commit statuses (`codesplitters/test`), so a GitHub PR shows them too.
4. **The UI and the merge gate.** Show checks on the branch page, the phone page (#426

text:
rustybuns init: prebuild steps behind run-p / npm-run-all are missed (create-vue's default build)
Follow-up to #403 (#413). `inferStaticBuild` (`packages/cli/src/glue/build-script.ts`) splits `build` on `&&` and inlines `<pm> run x`, but it doesn't look inside script runners.

create-vue's stock scripts:
```json
"build": "run-p type-check \"build-only {@}\" --",
"build-only": "node scripts/gen.mjs && vite build",
"type-check": "vue-tsc --build"
```
Checked on main (8c16d55): `inferStaticBuild` returns `{ pre: [], config: null }`. So `node scripts/gen.mjs` (and any `--config` on that vite) is missed, and a fresh clone's static build fails if it needs the generated file.

Parallel siblings like `type-check` can be left out. Add a unit test alongside the existing `inferStaticBuild` one in `test/init.test.ts`.

title: codeSplitters webhooks: a GitHub mode, so existing CI triggers fire from us (#532)
text:
codeSplitters webhooks: a GitHub-compatible mode so existing CI triggers fire from us
## Why

codeSplitters should be a **proxy to people's existing build setups**: the event source and scoreboard, while the build runs wherever it already runs (Jenkins, Buildkite, Argo, homegrown). It's also a hedge in case GitHub Actions gets pricier as agents run CI constantly: switching should mean changing a URL, not rewriting a pipeline.

`src/hooks.ts` already sends signed, retried, GitHub-*shaped* JSON, but not GitHub-*named*:

| ours | GitHub's |
|---|---|
| event `commit` | `push` |
| `branch.opened` | `create` |
| `branch.merged` | `pull_request` (closed, merged) |
| `X-CodeSplitters-Signature` | `X-Hub-Signature-256` |
| no event header | `X-GitHub-Event`, `X-GitHub-Delivery` |

Off-the-shelf receivers (the Jenkins GitHub plugin, Buildkite, Argo Events, Tekton triggers) switch on those headers, so they ignore us today.

## Scope

- A per-hook `github_compat: true` option. When it's on, deliveries use GitHub's event names and headers, and the payload fields those receivers actually read (`ref`, `before`, `after`, `repository.clone_url`, `head_commit`, `pull_request.*`).
- `clone_url` points at our git endpoint, so the receiver can fetch the sha.
- Keep the native names as 
codeSplitters webhooks: a GitHub mode, so existing CI triggers fire from us (#532)
Closes #532.

A hook made with `github_compat: true` (the **Speak GitHub** checkbox in the hooks panel) now speaks GitHub, so receivers built for GitHub webhooks (Jenkins GitHub plugin, Buildkite, Argo Events, Tekton) trigger on it as is. Native stays the default.

| | native | GitHub mode |
|---|---|---|
| events | `commit`, `branch.opened`, `branch.merged`, … | `push`, `create`, `pull_request`, `deployment_status`, `check_run` |
| headers | `X-CodeSplitters-Event/-Delivery/-Signature` | `X-GitHub-Event`, `X-GitHub-Delivery`, `X-Hub-Signature-256`, UA `GitHub-Hookshot/…` |
| fields added | |

text:
codeSplitters checks: a small GitHub-API shim so external CI can post statuses to us
## Why

This is the other half of the webhook compat mode (#532): results coming back. Many CI tools report to GitHub through a configurable "GitHub Enterprise" API base URL. If we answer the couple of endpoints they call, their status reporting lands in our checks (`checks.ts`) with no plugin to write.

## Scope

Mirror just the write paths under a compat prefix (for example `/gh/api/v3`):

- `POST /repos/:o/:r/statuses/:sha` becomes a check run, keyed by `context`. GitHub's `state` maps to ours: `pending`→running, `success`→passed, `failure`/`error`→failed.
- `POST /repos/:o/:r/check-runs` and `PATCH /repos/:o/:r/check-runs/:id` map to `recordRun` / `updateRun`.
- `GET /repos/:o/:r/commits/:sha/status` and `/check-runs`, because some tools read back what they wrote.
- Auth: a repo-scoped token sent as `Authorization: token …` / `Bearer …`, the way tools send a GitHub PAT.

Runs made this way get a new runner value, `external`, so they're told apart from `github` and our own runners. Required checks gate merges the same way.

Not the whole GitHub API: only what status reporters call.

- `POST /repos/:o/:r/statuses/:sha`: one run per `context`. `pending` maps to running, `success` to passed, `failure`/`error` to failed. Posting a finished context again starts a new run (a re-run).

title: codeSplitters checks: bring-your-own runners pull work, required checks scoped by path
text:
codeSplitters checks: bring-your-own runners pull work, and required checks scoped by path
## Why

A team's runners may live somewhere a webhook can't reach (behind a firewall, on a laptop, or on a build box with no inbound port). Those runners need to **pull** work rather than be pushed to. This makes "bring your own runner" a short loop anyone can wrap around their own build. It's the same model as GitHub's self-hosted runners, but without the agent binary.

Monorepos also need required checks that depend on what changed. `scripts/ci-apps.ts` does that by hand for RustyBuns, and GitHub's required checks are global and can't.

## Scope

1. **The claim protocol.**
   - `POST /api/repos/:o/:r/checks/claim {runner_label, names?}` atomically takes the oldest queued run that matches, marks it running, and returns `{id, ref, sha, name, clone_url, command?}`. It returns 204 when nothing is queued.
   - The runner streams output with the existing `PUT .../checks/:id {append}` and finishes with `{status, junit}`.
   - A run with no heartbeat for N minutes goes back to queued (pairs with #490).
2. **A reference runner script.** About 50 lines of Bun: claim, clone, run, report, loop. It's documented so it can be wrapped around Jenkins, Docker or anything else.
3. **Path-scoped req
codeSplitters checks: bring-your-own runners pull work, required checks scoped by path
Closes #534.

## What

**Claim protocol** (`src/checks.ts`, `migrations/0041_check_claims.sql`)
- `POST /api/repos/:o/:r/checks/claim {runner_label, names?}` (crew). A single conditional `UPDATE … WHERE id = (oldest queued) AND status = 'queued' RETURNING *` marks the run running, so when two runners race only one gets it. Returns `{id, ref, sha, name, clone_url, command?, stale_after_s}`, or 204 when nothing is queued.

title: Agent Office: /__rb/mem drops a pty host once it exits
text:
Agent Office: /__rb/mem keeps showing a pty host after it exits
Follow-up from #573 (#566).

Each floor's pty host writes its latest memory sample to `<floor>/.agent-office/pty-host-mem.json`, and the office's `/__rb/mem` reads that file. Nothing removes the file when the pty host exits. That happens when it's orphaned, unclaimed, or stopped. After that, `/__rb/mem` keeps reporting the dead host's last numbers as if it were still running. The `pid` and `at` fields are the only clue.

Fix: remove the file on exit (patch `ptyhost.js`'s exit paths, or `process.on('exit')` in `live/mem.ts`'s `ptyHostMem`). Or have `readPtyHostMem` treat a sample older than ~2 sampling intervals, or a pid that's gone, as `null`.
Agent Office: /__rb/mem drops a pty host once it exits
Closes #578.

A pty host left `pty-host-mem.json` behind when it exited, so `/__rb/mem` kept reporting the dead host's last numbers.

- `ptyHostMem` removes the file on `process.on('exit')`. That covers an orphaned, unclaimed or stopped host, or one that tripped the memory ceiling. It only removes the file if the file still holds its own pid.
- `readPtyHostMem` returns `null` when the sample's pid is no longer running (`kill(pid, 0)`). That covers a host killed by a signal, which skips exit handlers.

text:

Scale sideboard card **One D1 for the whole site** (#/admin/scale).

Every socket edit waits on a D1 write (`countHit` at `apps/codesplitters/src/file-do.ts:250`), and every request from the internet writes a `traffic` row (`src/insights.ts`). One D1 writes one query at a time, so the whole site tops out around ~500 writes/s (estimate), about 100 people typing at once.

codeSplitters: take the edit rate limit off D1
Closes #623. Follow-up for the traffic half: #638.

Found in the security audit (notes/SECURITY_AUDIT.md).

Nothing in the repo tells agents what they may not touch; AGENTS.md is about tests. Add a committed `.claude/settings.json` (and the AGENTS.md lines other harnesses read) with:

title: codeSplitters: collaborators can't un-hide lines or pass checks; agent tokens held to their repo
text:
codeSplitters: collaborators (agents too) can un-hide private lines, fake checks, and keep their token after removal
Found in the security audit (notes/SECURITY_AUDIT.md). Related: #618.

Repo-level permissions an invited collaborator, including an `agent-` handle, has today and probably shouldn't:

1. **Un-hiding private lines.** `POST …/do/private` only needs write (`src/worker.ts:346`). A collaborator can mark private lines public and commit, which publishes them to git and search. Make it owner-only.
2. **Recording checks.** `POST …/checks` lets any collaborator record a run with any `name` and `status` (`src/checks.ts:382`), which satisfies required checks in `mergeBlock`. Only a runner (CI token or the claimed runner) should be able to set a status, and a run recorded by a person should say so.
3. **Agent tokens.** An invite claimed `as: agent` mints a 30-day write token that works on every repo the agent can reach, and removing the collaborator leaves the token alive. Scope the token to the inviting repo and revoke it when the collaborator is removed.
4. **Handle squatting.** Adding a collaborator inserts the name into `users` (`src/worker.ts:310`), which reserves a handle nobody signed up for.

codeSplitters: collaborators can't un-hide lines or pass checks; agent tokens held to their repo
Closes #645.

All four items from the security audit:

1. **Un-hiding private lines is owner-only.** `POST …/do/private` with `private: false` is a 403 for anyone but the owner. The crew can still hide lines. A body without a boolean `private` is now a 400.
2. **Checks.** A collaborator's `POST …/checks` can only queue a run. It's labelled `by hand: @them` and its log says who recorded it. Only the owner can record a run with a status. Claiming a run stores `claimed_by`, and `PUT …/checks/:id` changes a status only for that claimer or the owner. Cancel is unchanged.

title: Local hosts: verify cached dylibs and office client, Host allowlist, /__rb/host passphrase strength
text:
Local hosts: verify cached dylibs and office client, Host allowlist, /__rb/host passphrase strength
Found in the security audit (notes/SECURITY_AUDIT.md).

- `packages/native/src/index.ts:46-60` dlopens any existing `~/.cache/rustybuns/<hash>-lib*.dylib` without checking it, and dev mode loads from `process.cwd()/native/dist`. A local process can plant a library. Check its sha256 against the embedded bytes before loading.
- Agent Office unpacks its client to `~/.cache/agent-office-rustybuns/<tag>-<hash>/public` and trusts it once `.ok` exists, so a local process can edit it and run script in the office page. Re-verify a manifest hash on start.
- `/__rb/host` accepts any hostname, `0.0.0.0` included, and any non-empty join passphrase. Require a passphrase of at least 12 characters (or generate one) when binding off loopback.
- The office checks Origin against Host but never checks Host against an allowlist (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, the configured host). Add one: it's the standard DNS-rebinding guard, belt and braces with the cookie.

Local hosts: verify cached dylibs and office client, Host allowlist, /__rb/host passphrase strength
Closes #651.

**Native dylibs** (`packages/native`): before every dlopen, a cached `~/.cache/rustybuns/<hash>-lib*.dylib` is compared byte for byte with the embedded one. If it differs, it's rewritten (tmp + rename), and the load fails if it still doesn't match. The cache dir is created 0700.

**Agent Office client**: the build hashes the client with sha256 and embeds the digest. Every start re-hashes the unpack, and a missing `.ok` or a mismatch unpacks it again from the binary (the bad copy is moved aside first).

title: Agent Office: workers.json keeps hashes of the hook tokens, and the guard refuses ps e (#642)
text:
Agent Office: any agent can read every worker's hook token, the pty token and the office session secret
Found in the security audit (notes/SECURITY_AUDIT.md).

Every agent runs as the same macOS user as the office, so 0600 files don't separate them. Any worker can read:

- `<repo>/.agent-office/workers.json`: **every** worker's `hookToken`, so it can call the hook port as any other worker (send_home, tell_worker, link_pr in their name).
- `<repo>/.agent-office/pty-host.json` + `pty.sock`: the pty host token, so it can type into any terminal, shells included (this gets around tell_worker's refusal to message shells).
- `~/agent-office/.agent-office/config.json`: the session-signing `secret` and, until shown, the generated `password` in plaintext, which is enough to forge an office session.

Verified: an agent in a worktree could list those files' keys.

- Give each worker only its own hook token (env), and keep the map of tokens in memory or hashed on disk.
- Keep the session secret and password in the macOS Keychain (`security add-generic-password`) rather than config.json; drop the plaintext password once it's hashed.
- Put the pty socket and token somewhere workers aren't pointed at, and add a PreToolUse hook (see the agent rules is

**Cause.** The repo page's **Checks run** select saved as soon as its `change` event fired. title: Agent Office: Merge when ready waits for CI, office:update swaps the office (#602, #603)
text:
Agent Office: "Merge when ready" merges straight away on RustyBuns
Agent Office's ⏱ Merge when ready runs `gh pr merge <n> --squash --auto` and leaves the waiting to GitHub. On this repo GitHub has nothing to wait for:

- `main` has no branch protection and no rulesets, so no check is required.
- A PR with CI still running is `UNSTABLE`, and gh merges `CLEAN`, `HAS_HOOKS` and `UNSTABLE` PRs right away instead of turning on auto-merge (cli/cli `pkg/cmd/pr/merge/merge.go`, `isImmediatelyMergeable`, v2.102.0).
- `allow_auto_merge` is false anyway.

So the PR merges before CI finishes, a failing PR can land, and the office toasts "set PR #n to merge once its checks pass", which isn't true.

Fix (repo settings):
- A ruleset on `main` requiring the `typecheck` and `apps` checks.
- Settings → General → Allow auto-merge.

Then a PR with checks running shows as `BLOCKED` and `--auto` queues it until CI passes. Note this blocks plain merges of red PRs too.

Do together with the next issue (office:update restarting the office), in one PR where code is involved.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
Agent Office: office:update restarts the office itself (workers survive a SIGTERM)
`bun run office:update` pulls and rebuilds, but when the office is already up it only says "stop it and run this again", and its comment says stopping it ends every worker's session.

That's only true for Ctrl+C. Upstream treats SIGTERM as a restart (`server/cli.js`): the workers' terminals live in a detached pty host, and the next office picks them back up with their scrollback. Tested on a throwaway office: across a swap the office process changed, while the pty host and a running worker kept the same PIDs, didn't miss a tick, and the new office showed the full screen from before.

So `office:update` can rebuild, SIGTERM the running office and start the new one itself. The swap is already written as `office:mama` (apps/agent-office/scripts/mama.ts, not yet merged): watch bun, bun.lock, package.json and the pinned release; rebuild while the old office runs; keep the old one if the build fails; restart a crashed office with backoff. Ship mama with this, possibly as a flag on `office:update` rather than its own script, and fix the outdated comment.

text:

Found in the security audit (notes/SECURITY_AUDIT.md).

`childEnv()` hands each worker and pty the office's whole `process.env`, minus a few nested-session vars. Whatever is in the shell that started the office (a `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, `GH_TOKEN`, `OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN`, an LLM key) reaches every agent.

Every edit rewrites the whole file into one key (`put("doc")`, `apps/codesplitters/src/file-do.ts:208`). A DO storage value is capped at 2 MB, so a file of ~15–20k lines stops saving, and big files cost more to write as they grow.

title: codeSplitters: hosted deploys wait for the owner's review; the doctor's code runs apart from the agent's keys (#646)
text:
codeSplitters: deploys and the dependency doctor run collaborator code next to the owner's keys
Found in the security audit (notes/SECURITY_AUDIT.md).

`DeployRunner` unseals the repo owner's deploy key (Cloudflare / Railway / Hetzner) into a container that runs the repo's install and Alchemy code with internet access. Any collaborator, agents included, who gets code onto main has that code run with the owner's key on the next deploy. The output hider only masks the exact string, so an encoded key gets out.

Similarly, the hosted agent sandbox runs the dependency doctor's `install` (lifecycle scripts) in the same container as the harness's LLM keys. Blanking them from the child env isn't a boundary (same UID, `/proc/<pid>/environ`).

Proposals:
- A deploy whose diff since the last deploy includes commits by someone other than the owner waits for the owner to approve it in the UI (show the diff).
- Install with `--ignore-scripts` in both containers, then run what's needed explicitly; run installs in a separate container from the keys.
- Narrow egress where Containers allow it.

title: codeSplitters: apply() and replay() are linear on a big batch (#684)
text:
codeSplitters scale: apply() is quadratic on a big batch of inserts
Found while working on #624. `apply`/`step` in `apps/codesplitters/src/lines.ts` does `doc.lines.findIndex` for each op, so one batch of 40k inserts each after the last takes several seconds (40k × 40k). A big paste or import into a file, or a merge of a big branch, pays this. Next step: keep a line-id → index map for the batch, or look up from the last insert's position first.
codeSplitters: apply() and replay() are linear on a big batch (#684)
Closes #684.

`step` (under `apply`) and `replay` looked up each op's line with `findIndex` from the top, so a batch of N inserts each after the last cost N². Now a small `locate()` in `src/lines.ts` scans outward from the last line the batch touched. A paste, a top-to-bottom diff or a block delete finds its line in one or two looks. A batch in random order costs no more than it did before.

40k-line file, timed locally (ms):

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| paste (40k inserts) | 3506 | 17 |
| set every other line | 1631 | 11 |
| delete 30k-line block | 140 | 127 |
| replay all of it | 65

text:
codeSplitters scale: range-read the op log, snapshot and trim
Scale sideboard card **The op log is read whole**.

`log(since)` (`apps/codesplitters/src/file-do.ts:222`) lists every `op:` key and then filters, and nothing trims the log. A long-lived hot file (~300k ops, estimate) runs the DO into the 128 MB isolate limit on reconnect or time travel.

Next step: list from `op:<since>` with a start key, snapshot, and trim old ops.
codeSplitters: range-read the op log, snapshot and trim (#625)
Closes #625.

A file's op log was listed whole on every `log`, time travel and commit, and never trimmed, so a long-lived hot file could run its Durable Object into the 128 MB limit.

- **Range reads.** `log(since)` lists from `op:<since+1>`, 1,000 ops a page, instead of every `op:` key.
- **Snapshots.** Every 2,000 ops the doc is saved as `snap:<rev>`, in chunks like the doc. Time travel replays from the nearest snapshot, so it replays at most about 2,000 ops.
- **Trim.** The file keeps ten snapshots. When an eleventh lands, the oldest is deleted and history starts at the next one (`trimmed`)

title: codeSplitters: trim a file's existing long log at its first snapshot (#707)
text:
codeSplitters scale: trim a file's existing long log sooner
Follow-up to #625. Trimming starts once a file has 10 snapshots (one every 2,000 ops), so a file that already has a long untrimmed log keeps all of it until 20,000 more edits land. Until then `GET do/log?since=0` still returns all of it, in pages of 1,000 but collected in one response (time travel and commits are fine: they replay from a snapshot or read only from the last commit).

Options: on the first snapshot of a file whose rev is well past KEEP_SNAPS * SNAP_EVERY, trim straight to that snapshot. Or page the log API with a `limit` and next cursor.

title: codeSplitters dependency doctor: 0.0.x and 0.x bumps get semver's level (#697)
text:
codeSplitters dependency doctor: ^0.0.x and exact 0.x bumps are labelled patch, but semver treats them as breaking
Found while running the doctor on RustyBuns (#615). `levelOf()` in `apps/codesplitters/src/deps.ts` compares major/minor/patch literally. So `@tscircuit/core` 0.0.1929 → 0.0.2112 counts as a **patch**, and so does `^0.0.599` → `^0.0.617`, which means they pass `max_level: "patch"` or `"minor"`. Under semver (and how `^` reads them), every 0.0.x change is breaking, and so is a 0.x minor.

Suggested fix: shift the level for leading zeros (0.0.x: any change is major; 0.x.y: a minor change is major and a patch is minor), with a test.

title: Agent Office: send_home, tell_worker and office-workers stop trusting every agent (#644)
text:
Agent Office: send_home, tell_worker and the office-workers CLI trust every agent on the floor
Found in the security audit (notes/SECURITY_AUDIT.md).

The office's agent-to-agent tools trust every worker on the floor:

- `send_home` with an explicit `cleanup: "worktree"|"all"` runs `git worktree remove --force --force`, which throws away another agent's uncommitted work. The default `auto` is safe. Proposal: refuse forced cleanup of another worker's dirty tree unless a human clicks it, or WIP-commit it first.
- `tell_worker` sends up to 20k characters of prompt to any other agent and wakes stopped ones. A prompt-injected agent can pass the injection on. Proposal: show the text on the receiving desk as "from <worker>", and let the user switch on "ask me first" for tell_worker and hire_worker.
- The MCP tools go through Claude Code's permission prompt, but the `office-workers` CLI and a `curl` to the hook port with `$AGENT_OFFICE_HOOK_TOKEN` do the same over Bash with no prompt. Proposal: the same confirmation server-side, so every path gets it.

Closes #644.

Every agent-to-agent path (the `agent-office` MCP tools, the `office-workers` command, a `curl` to the hook port with `$AGENT_OFFICE_HOOK_TOKEN`) lands in one upstream handler, `server/hooks/office-workers.js`. So the guards are patched in there, server-side, and every path gets them. That covers the issue's third point.

- **send_home**: a forced cleanup (`worktree` or `all`) of a worker whose worktree has uncommitted or unpushed work (or can't be checked) falls back to `auto`. The worker still goes home and its worktree stays. The result carries `held: "Kept X's worktree: it ha

title: codeSplitters desktop: the primary git store, local out and GitHub in (#464)
text:
codeSplitters desktop: the primary git store, local out and GitHub in
Part of dogfooding: codeSplitters hosts codeSplitters (and RustyBuns), with GitHub as the backup. Sibling issues: the build/CI runner (#463) and the integration (#465).

## What

Today a desktop mirror is GitHub-first: codeSplitters keeps a copy and syncs with upstream. This issue flips that around: **local out, cloud in.** The desktop's bare repos in `~/.codesplitters` are the source of truth, and GitHub is a remote that gets pushed to as the backup and as the trigger for the existing Actions pipeline.

It works like Agent Office, which gives every worker its own local git worktree. codeSplitters becomes another git store that agents, runners and your own tools check out from.

## Scope

1. **Primary per mirror.** A mirror setting `primary: "here" | "upstream"`. With "here", sync pushes first, and a clash defaults to Keep mine but still asks. `src/mirror.ts` already does both directions and never force-pushes; this changes who leads, not the plumbing.
2. **Real checkouts.** A worktree per branch, or per agent run / check run, made with `git worktree add` off the bare repo, so agents and the runner (#463) work in a real directory. Remove them when the branch merges or the run ends.

With `"here"`, a sync with commits waiting pushes them first and fetches nothing. Only when that push is turned away because upstream moved does it fall back to fetch, merge, push. title: codeSplitters checks: install dependencies before a package.json plan runs (#775)
text:
codeSplitters checks: install dependencies before a package.json plan runs
Follow-up to #750.

Our runners (scripts/runner.ts, the desktop's in-process runner, and the CiRunner container) clone the repo and run the check's command as it stands. The plans built from package.json (`bun run test`, and the per-workspace `cd apps/x && bun run test`) assume dependencies are installed, and a fresh clone has no node_modules. So any repo with dependencies fails these checks, and RustyBuns's apps fail because workspace packages don't resolve.

Options: have the plan prefix an install picked from the lockfile (`bun install --frozen-lockfile`, `npm ci`, ...), or have the runner install once per clone before the command. The container's egress already allows the npm and yarn registries.

A runner's fresh clone has no node_modules, so checks planned from package.json (`bun run test`, `cd apps/x && bun run test`) failed on any repo with dependencies.

**What changed**
- `planFrom` takes an optional `install` command and starts every package.json-derived check with it, at the root: `bun install --frozen-lockfile && cd 'apps/a' && bun run test`.
- `planChecks` picks the install from the files at the ref's root (main's tree, plus whatever the branch adds or deletes there): `bun install --frozen-lockfile` when there's a `bun.lock`/`bun.lockb`, otherwise `bun install`.

title: codeSplitters: created_at / updated_at on the tables that lack them (#747)
text:
codeSplitters: created_at / updated_at on the tables that lack them
From #512's comment: "a lot of tables should have a createdAt updatedAt; it makes a lot of diagnosing things easier, like telling that something got overwritten here." #739 added `users.created_at`. Here's what's still missing, checked against the migrated schema:

**No creation time:** collaborators, files, branch_files, playlists, tracks, handle_grants, deploy_settings, check_settings, check_watches, dep_watches, limit_rules, limit_hits, levels, level_parts, git_pending, fresh_objects, watch_state (and caches: blob_lines, fit_cache, tree_cache, walls_cache).

**Rows that get updated in place but have no updated time:** users (bio, theme, pulse, git_truth), repos (visibility, settings), deploy_settings, check_settings, webhooks, playlists, collaborators (role changes), limit_rules.

title: codeSplitters desktop: a push to the bare repo lands in the files open here (#773)
text:
codeSplitters desktop: a push to the bare repo is undone by the next commit of a file open here
Found while doing #464, which adds a **Push back** remote so your own tools can push to a desktop repo's bare git.

## What happens

A push from outside the app (a terminal, an editor, Agent Office) moves `refs/heads/main` in the bare repo, but the files open here as lines (their Durable Objects) never hear about it. The next commit of such a file from the app writes its stale lines over the pushed change. The pushed commit stays in history, but the tip loses the change, and the next mirror sync carries that loss upstream.

Repro (the same shape as the `primary here` test in `apps/codesplitters/test/mirror.test.ts`):

1. A mirror with README open here (edited and committed once).
2. Clone the repo through the `push` remote, change README's second line, commit and push to `codesplitters main`.
3. Sync: upstream has the terminal's line. The README Durable Object still has the old one.
4. Edit and commit README's first line here, then sync: upstream's README is back to the old second line.

New files from a push (ones not open here) are fine.

## Fix sketch

The mirror sync already lands upstream's commits into open files as line edits (`liveChanges` + `land` in `src/mirror.ts`, merge

title: codeSplitters desktop: a push that clashes with edits here holds that file's commit (#788)
text:
codeSplitters desktop: a push that clashes with edits not committed here is still undone by the next commit
Follow-up to #773.

landPushes (`apps/codesplitters/src/mirror.ts`) lands commits pushed to a desktop repo's bare git in the files open here. A file with edits here that aren't committed yet gets the push merged in with `merge3`. Where both touch the same lines, or the push changes a line right beside an edit here (merge3 is strict about neighbours), the edits here stand and nothing tells you. Then the next commit of that file here writes over the pushed lines, as before #773.

Two more gaps:

- **No baseline yet.** `repos.git_seen` starts NULL. The first look takes main's tip as it stands, so a push made before the app's first commit or look at that repo isn't landed.
- **Nothing on screen.** A push only reaches an open file when it's opened or committed again, or at a sync (mirrors only). A page left open doesn't hear of it.

Possible fix: make such a clash visible, like a mirror's `clash` state, and offer to take the pushed side. Start the baseline when a repo is made or cloned on the desktop.

text:
Cost guards: MCP tool calls count against rate limits; GitHub Actions stay free
Real barriers against a surprise bill, from a survey of everything in the repo that can spend money.

## 1. codeSplitters: MCP skipped every rate limit

`/api/mcp` replays each tool call as a new `Request` carrying only the token (`mcp.ts` `toRequest`). `counted()` only counts requests stamped with `cf-connecting-ip`, so every tool call went uncounted. Anyone who signed up and made a write token could call `create_repo`, `commit_file`, `fork_level` (Artifacts imports) and `search_code` (Workers AI embeddings, with vectors on) without limit. Found while surveying what can run up a bill (#796 fixed the worst one: MCP tool calls skipped every rate limit). These gaps remain in code:

1. **Hosted agent runs have no hard cap** (admin-only).
   - `HOSTED_RUN_MS` (15 minutes, `src/agent-routes.ts:82`) is only shown as a deadline (`:101`). Nothing stops a run when it passes.

- Queues `codesplitters-hooks`, `codesplitters-jobs`, `codesplitters-level-digs`

The copy scripts and config can be a PR. The live copy and the deploy are the owner's (see #806 for the state move that has to come first).

Nothing is broken today: the names only show in the Cloudflare dashboard.

title: codeSplitter: the release script moves into the repo, tested; --move copies only after you say deploy
text:
MANUAL RUN: copy codeSplitter's data to the codesplitter names and deploy (#809)
After #809's PR merges, the next deploy has to move the data with it. Until then, any deploy is refused: it would replace `codesplitters-db`, the three queues and the bucket, and the Alchemy state is still under the old app name.

In your checkout, at a quiet time, with each step done before the next:

```sh
cd ~/Documents/projects/RustyBuns && git pull && bun install
cd apps/codesplitter
CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID=<codeSplitter account id> bun scripts/move-resources.ts
```

That one only reads. It should end "Nothing in the way". If it stops, it says why (a Vectorize index that exists, say). In the dashboard, check that the queues `codesplitters-hooks`, `codesplitters-jobs` and `codesplitters-level-digs` have a backlog of 0. Then:

```sh
CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID=<id> bun scripts/move-resources.ts --copy
CODESPLITTER_DEPLOYS=1 CODESPLITTER_AGENTS=1 CODESPLITTER_CHECKS=1 bunx rustybuns plan
```

The copy ends with "codesplitter-db matches codesplitters-db". The plan should warn that D1 DB, the queues HOOKS, JOBS and LEVEL_DIGS, and R2 LEVEL_CHUNKS are renamed, and create or delete nothing else. **Stop if it wants to create the Worker or a container**: that means the state didn't move. title: Agent Office: why our add-ons keep their own three (#839)
text:
Agent Office: our add-ons could use the office's own three
After #838, the office loads two copies of three r186: Agent Office's own, inlined in `main-*.js`, and ours, in `/assets/rb-chunk-*.js`, which the Druids skin and the codeSplitter tiles share. So the console still prints `THREE.WARNING: Multiple instances of Three.js being imported.` once, and the page downloads about 400 KB it doesn't need.

The office's bundle doesn't export three, and there's no namespace object we could pick it up from. Getting down to one copy would mean either:

- patching `main-*.js` to hand its three classes to `globalThis`, which is fragile on minified code, or
- asking upstream (AgentSystemLabs/agent-office) to expose three, for example as a separate chunk or `window.THREE`. Per our rules, that only happens if the owner asks.

It's harmless as it is. Three checks `isMesh`-style flags, not `instanceof`, so objects work across the two copies.

text:
codeSplitter: let a dug fork listen to its upstream
A dug fork (a GitHub repo or a level, forked into a git repo here) keeps `upstream` and `upstream_commit`, then never looks at upstream again. Only a **mirror** listens, and mirrors need git on the machine: the desktop, not the live site.

The git map (the PR that adds it) now draws this as a dashed "copied once" curve. The next step is to let a fork listen:

- **Hear:** for a `github:` upstream, ask GitHub's compare API (`upstream_commit...<default branch>`) every so often (on the hourly cron, or when the repo page opens), and keep `behind` and the newest upstream sha.

- **Turn it into a mirror** on the desktop: a fork you dug up there could become a two-way mirror in one click.

title: watch: give changeCheck 1s of clock slack for new files (#853)
text:
watch: changeCheck can miss a file created just after it starts (flaky on Linux CI)
`packages/cli/test/watch.test.ts` › "changeCheck: a file that was only read is not a change; a write, a new file or a delete is" failed once on Linux CI (#852, run 38220213996, `Expected: true, Received: false`), and passes locally and on rerun.

Likely cause, in `changeCheck()` (`packages/cli/src/watch.ts`): a file seen for the first time counts as a change only if `mtime >= since`, where `since = Date.now()`. Linux stamps mtimes from the kernel's coarse clock, which can be a few ms behind `Date.now()`, so a file created right after the check starts can look older than `since` and get missed. The test creates `new.ts` within the same millisecond window. The watcher has the same race: a file saved just after `build desktop --watch` starts could be skipped.

Fix idea: give `since` some slack (say, a 1s margin), or record first-seen files as changes when they weren't there at the start.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

watch: give changeCheck 1s of clock slack for new files (#853)
Closes #853.

`changeCheck()` counted a first-seen file as a change only if `mtime >= since`. Linux stamps mtimes from the kernel's coarse clock, which can trail `Date.now()` by a few ms, so a file created right after the check started could be missed: the flaky CI failure in `watch.test.ts`, and the same race for a save just after `build desktop --watch` starts.

Now a new file counts if its mtime is within 1 s (`CLOCK_SLACK_MS`) of the start. The read-only case is unaffected: it's about files that already existed, and those are compared by mtime and size.

title: Local twins: enforce the D1, KV, queue and DO edge limits
text:
Local twins: enforce the edge limits slim borg found them looser on
Slim borg's `--limits` grid (from #855) shows the local twins accept everything the edge refuses, on both the desktop and box hosts:

| Limit | Edge | Twin |
|---|---|---|
| `d1-params` | 100 bound parameters | 101 accepted (bun:sqlite allows 32766) |
| `kv-key` | 512-byte keys | 513 accepted |
| `queue-size` | 128 KB messages | 140 KB accepted |
| `do-value` | 2 MB values (SQLite-backed) | 3 MB accepted |
| `memory` | 128 MB per isolate | 200 MB accepted |
| `cpu` | 10 ms Free / `cpuMs` on Paid | no limit |

So an app can pass every local check and then fail on its first deploy. The first four are cheap to enforce in `packages/shell-bun/src/bindings` (throw with the edge's message). Memory and CPU are harder: a warning in dev, or honouring `worker.cpuMs`, may be enough.

When a twin enforces one, add it to `ENFORCED` in `apps/borg/test/local.test.ts`.

title: codeSplitter line locks: an agent rests 2 minutes after its claim hits its cap
text:
codeSplitter line locks: an agent can re-claim its lines right after its 30-minute cap
Follow-up from #926 (line locks phase 1).

An agent's claim can't be renewed past its cap (30 minutes from when it was laid, unless a person sends `extend`). But once the claim lapses at the cap, the same agent can call `claim_lines` again with the lines and get a new claim with a new cap, before anyone else has had a chance at them. The heartbeat in `agent-run.ts` can't do this (it renews by id alone, which is a 400 once the claim is gone). A hand-written MCP client could, though.

Options:
- remember the ids of claims that hit their cap for a short grace window, and refuse a re-claim from the same holder on those lines during it
- or let phase 2's queue (`claim_lines {wait: true}`) handle it: at the cap, waiters get the lines first

See `apps/codesplitter/docs/line-locks.md`, phase 2.

title: trial-github: flag suspicious behaviour (install scripts, blocked network, busy idle hosts, malicious deps)
text:
trial-github: flag suspicious behaviour (install scripts, blocked network, CPU spikes) in the report
The harness contains strangers' code: no logins, committed secrets deleted, no remote build steps, and on macOS sandbox-exec with no network after install and no access to the real home. Containment is the defense, because reading code can't reliably catch malware.

On top of that, the report should flag behaviour worth a human look, as a ⚠️ beside the app:
- **Install scripts:** which dependencies (and the app) run pre- or postinstall scripts.
- **Blocked network attempts during build or boot:** a build has no reason to phone home. sandbox-exec denials show up in the unified log (`log show --predicate 'eventMessage contains "deny"'`), so collect the ones from each step's pid.
- **Reads outside the clone** that the sandbox denied (~/.ssh, keychains).
- **Unusual CPU or memory at boot** (miners). `--prof` already measures both.
- **Known-bad dependencies** from an advisory feed (OSV) for the lockfile.

Nothing flagged is published, and strangers' binaries never leave the sandbox either way.

Design: `apps/codesplitter/docs/merge-solutions.md`, §3. Measured on the 29 git hunks between main and #893 and #886: today's merge by line id settles 16, and this settles 25.

text:

Follow-up from #933. The ordering rule (both sides add at one spot: main's first, or sorted if the base list was sorted) is in for items inside one line: `mergeWords(…, both)` puts `import { a, b, c, d, z }` in order. text:

Design: `apps/codesplitter/docs/merge-solutions.md`, §6 and §7.

- `conflict-agent.ts` runs only on what L1–L3 leave, which was 3 of 29 hunks in the measurement. It gets the hunk, both sides' commit messages and the already-settled merge of the rest of the file.

- **JSON both sides parse that the merge breaks.** Once every other line is settled, this becomes a `lint:json` conflict. A file that didn't parse to begin with, like a tsconfig with comments, isn't held.

text:

Design: apps/codesplitter/docs/line-locks.md (#925). Follows phase 1.

- `claim_lines {wait: true}`: FIFO per file, a socket `grant` with a 15 s grant window, and MCP/CLI long-polls capped at about 20 s (an open request keeps the DO awake, which bills duration)

title: excalibrawl: the pen, a token-cheap drawing language for text-model fighters (#985)
text:
Excalibrawl: the pen, a token-cheap drawing language for text-model fighters
A follow-up to #970 and #981, picked up from a conversation with the owner. Nothing here is built yet.

## Why

The bake-off (#981, results in `apps/excalibrawl/README.md`) found three things:

- **Arithmetic is the weak spot.** Models do worst at coordinate maths, and parts float apart.
- **The tooling is expensive.** The original site's JSON ops cost about 60 tokens a shape, plus about 900 tokens of instructions.
- **Clef can't write.** It only answers questions, so it can't be the creative fighter.

The aim is an intelligence-meets-creativity test. Give text models a small, cheap "pen" for Excalidraw, prefer compact commands over MCP-style schemas, and see what they do with a few powerful moves. Clef becomes the referee.

## The pen (draft tool card, about 200 tokens)

```
EXCALIDRAW PEN · canvas 700×700, x right, y down · one command per line · later lines draw on top
Shapes, named so you can refer back to them:
  o NAME X Y W H COLOR      ellipse, centred at X Y
  b NAME X Y W H COLOR      box
  d NAME X Y W H COLOR      diamond
  p NAME COLOR X,Y X,Y …    filled polygon (ears, hats, beaks, roofs)
  l NAME COLOR X,Y X,Y …    stroke (tails, arms, smiles, hair)
  t NAME X Y SIZE
excalibrawl: the pen, a token-cheap drawing language for text-model fighters (#985)
Closes #985.

## What's in it

- **`src/engine/pen.ts`, the pen.** Pen text becomes `SkeletonEl` ops. It covers `o`/`b`/`d`/`p`/`l`/`t`, the edits `mv`/`sz`/`fill`/`rm`/`up`, and `look`/`done`. A name you draw again gets redrawn. Anchors (`.top .bottom .left .right .c`, with an optional `±dx,dy` or just `±dx`) sit on the bounding box. Ids are prefixed per fighter, so one fighter can't anchor to another's shapes. Each line runs through `applyOps` as it's read, so an anchor sees the clamped position. A bad line is skipped with a reason. Lines over the cap of 8 are skipped too, and `look`, `done`

title: codeSplitter docs: CI for your public repo, on your own machine (#978)
text:
codeSplitter marketing: CI on your own hardware for a public repo, with no path in for fork PRs
Pitch codeSplitter's one-way mirror plus CiRunner as **"run CI for your public repo on your own hardware, with no path in for strangers."**

## The use case

A public GitHub repo, mirrored one way into codeSplitter. codeSplitter's CiRunner hands jobs to a machine you own (a spare Mac at home, say), which **pulls** them. Nothing on that machine listens for incoming connections.

- **Fork PRs never get in.** They stay on GitHub and never mirror, so a stranger's `.github/workflows` edit can't reach your box. That's the usual reason GitHub warns against self-hosted runners on public repos, and personal accounts can't restrict runners to workflows (that needs an organization's runner groups).
- **Only trusted code runs:** merged `main`, which you reviewed, plus your own and your agents' branches pushed to codeSplitter.
- **Your hardware:** native builds, long sweeps and big test matrices run on the machine you already own. GitHub's free runners keep doing quick PR checks.

## Honest framing

It's not new in kind. It's the pull model that big teams already use:
- GitLab's "CI/CD for external repos" (pull mirroring from GitHub plus GitLab runners)
- Buildkite (agents on your machines poll

title: codeSplitter: policy per path, with defaults a repo overrides in .gitattributes (#938)
text:
codeSplitter: the platform runs the merge loop, agents fill the gaps (tracking)
Agents will crowd the same files. That's a given. codeSplitter should let them, with the policy in code: **the platform runs the loop, and agents fill only the gaps it can't decide.** Today an agent coordinates by prompt, one judgment at a time. That's what the PR agent did all of 2026-10-12, and it still got a merge order wrong once.

## The loop, owned by codeSplitter

1. **Queue live.** Agents claim a line or range, wait in line for a hot one, and announce intents. Nobody piles on, so conflicts don't start. #926 (leases), #927 (waiting line, soft intents).
2. **Stack what doesn't compete.** Merge by line id lands non-overlapping lines and files. Branches land oldest first, each against main as the last merge left it (#903). Deterministic rules settle "both only added to it": #933 (list and paragraph one-liners), conventions #935.
3. **Only real problems go to someone.** A build-checked AI fallback, then a person. #934 (also refuses conflict markers).
4. **Offline people.** Their choice. On reconnect their edits replay onto line ids, and a stale edit is rebased word by word instead of rejected (#928).
5. **Self-healing CI.** A failure or a guard trip opens a fix task on that bran

title: shell-bun: priority classes with adaptive backoff; trial harness runs as low (#955)
text:
Priority classes for Rusty Buns work: realtime / high / normal / low, with adaptive backoff
Idea from the owner while trial runs hogged a laptop: let work on a Rusty Buns host declare a priority, and have the host schedule it.

- **realtime:** never touched. Think a DJ doing live audio: an AudioWorklet, a game loop, a live session. The scheduler never preempts or throttles it, and keeps headroom for it.
- **high:** user-facing requests.
- **normal:** most work.
- **low:** builds, sweeps, indexing, nightly jobs. It runs wide when the machine is idle and backs off when a sustained spike in CPU or memory appears (not a blip: a window long enough and high enough), then ramps back up.

Effect is a natural fit: per-class semaphores whose permits are resized by a sampler (load average, the host's memWatch, rss), `Effect.interruptible` low-priority fibers that yield at checkpoints, and `Schedule` for backoff and ramp-up. The host already has memWatch and cpuProfile, and queues and crons already run in-process, so those are the first users: a cron or queue consumer is `low` unless it says otherwise. Child processes (the trial harness's installs and builds) get OS priority too (`nice`/`taskpolicy -b` on macOS, so the kernel prefers everything else).

TypeError: ECONNRESET: The socket connection was closed unexpectedly
  path: "http://127.0.0.1:45097/__rb/host"
```

Seen in CI (run 38231777663, attempt 1, job "packages") and once locally in 90 parallel runs of the file.

## Why

`rebind()` in `packages/shell-bun/src/serve.ts` calls `server.stop(false)` on the old listener and opens a new one on the same port. The client's keep-alive pool still holds an idle connection to the old listener, at the same host:port. The old server closes it as it stops, and a request sent on it in that moment is reset. A POST isn't safely retryable, so the host page's next control request (or a guest's) can fail the same way right after "Host a world" or "Stop hosting".

## Ideas

- After a rebind, answer with `Connection: close` (on the rebind response itself), so the client doesn't reuse a socket on the listener that's going away.
- Or let the old server finish requests al
shell-bun: Connection: close from a listener that rebind replaced (#975)
Closes #975.

`rebind()` stops the old listener with `stop(false)`, which closes each keep-alive connection on it once it goes idle, with no warning. A client that sends its next request the moment the rebind response lands (the host page's next `POST /__rb/host`, or the multiplayer test) has the socket closed under it: ECONNRESET.

- `serve.ts`: the request body moves into `respond()`. The listener's `fetch` adds `Connection: close` to any response from a listener `rebind()` has replaced, the rebind's own response included, so the client drops that socket and opens a new one on the new listen

title: codeSplitter checks: run here on main commits a mirror takes from upstream (#1008)
text:
codeSplitter checks: run on main commits a mirror takes from upstream
From #1003, a gap in the "CI for your public repo, on your own machine" pitch (#978).

When a one-way mirror takes new commits on main from upstream, codeSplitter doesn't run its own checks on them. In `settled()`, queue `startChecks(..., "main", tip, "upstream")` when checks run here, so merged upstream code gets tested on your machine.

Related: #978, #1003.

codeSplitter checks: run here on main commits a mirror takes from upstream
Found while checking #978's pitch against the code (PR #1003).

When a mirror takes upstream's new commits on main, `settled()` in `apps/codesplitter/src/mirror.ts` calls `upstreamMoved()`, which only watches GitHub's Actions results for the new tip. Nothing is queued here, so with checks set to run `here` or `both`, merged `main` from GitHub never runs on your own runner or the desktop.

Checks start here today on: a commit made here (`worker.ts`, `pick.ts`), a branch opened from upstream, pulled or pushed (`mirror.ts`), and a beam.

## Fix

In `settled()`, when the tip moved because of upstream, also queue here (`startChecks(env, owner, repo, "main", tip, "upstream")`, or have `upstreamMoved` queue when `s.here`). Test: a mirror with `where: "here"` that takes an upstream commit gets a queued run at that sha.

title: Priority scheduler: worker threads and a warm pool (#1047)
text:
Priority scheduler: warm pool and worker threads (after #1028)
Carried over from #1028. The scheduler (`packages/shell-bun/src/priority.ts`) now stops hung jobs, measures child processes and requeues them when memory runs short. Two items from that issue are still to do:

- **A `warm: n` pool** of loaded workers or processes, so short jobs skip Bun's startup. A pooled worker holds memory while it is idle, so the pool has to count against the memory budget and shrink when the sampler backs off.
- **CPU-heavy JS on worker threads**, run through the same slots: something like `scheduler.worker(priority, url, data)`. A stop (timeout, memory) would `terminate()` the worker. That makes it the first job a stop really interrupts, since plain JS that ignores its `signal` runs on. The pool above would hand these out.

Both need a real user first, such as a trial step or a build step that is CPU-bound in JS, so the pool size and the startup saved can be measured rather than guessed.

Priority scheduler: worker threads and a warm pool (#1047)
Closes #1047.

`packages/shell-bun/src/priority.ts`:

- **`scheduler.worker(priority, url, data, opts)`** runs CPU-heavy JS on a worker thread in the same slots as `run` and `spawn`. The data is posted to the module at `url`, and the first message it sends back is the result. It takes `timeoutMs`, `memMb` and `requeues` like other jobs, plus `transfer`. A stop **terminates the thread**, so this is the first JS job that a stop actually interrupts. A worker that throws is terminated and its job rejects.
