title: codeSplitter: a branch push or desktop beam writes one trailing newline, as main does (#1041)
text:
codeSplitter: a branch push or desktop beam adds a blank last line to files written with a trailing newline
Found while building #1024.

`branchTree` in `apps/codesplitter/src/mirror.ts` (used by `pushBranch`, and by a desktop beam of a codeSplitter branch since #1026) writes each branch file with `toDisk(doc.lines)`, which always adds a `\n`. Main's commits write the same lines another way (`archive.ts` `pushCatalogues`): joined, and a `\n` only when the text doesn't already end in one.

A file written through the API with content ending in a newline (`POST /api/repos/:o/:r/files {content: "stays\n"}`) keeps an empty last line. Main commits it as `stays\n`, but `branchTree` writes `stays\n\n`. So a branch push upstream, or a desktop beam, adds a blank line at the end of such a file that nobody wrote.

The hosted beam (#1024) uses main's rule. `branchTree` should use it too. The desktop codeSplitter-branch beam test in `test/beam.test.ts` misses this because its `sh` helper trims output.

title: Priority scheduler: checkpoints that yield and stop, Effect jobs a stop interrupts (#1048)
text:
Priority scheduler: interruptible fibers with checkpoints, on Effect (after #1028)
Carried over from #1028. A scheduler job can now be stopped. Its `JobContext.signal` aborts on a timeout or a memory stop, and `spawn()` kills the child. In-process JS only stops if it checks the signal, though, and it never yields its slot partway through.

- **Fibers that can be interrupted, and yield at checkpoints.** A long job would give its slot back at a checkpoint when higher-priority work is waiting, then wait for it again. A stop would actually interrupt it, instead of leaving it to run on outside the budget.
- **Move the scheduler to Effect** (semaphores per class, `Schedule` for the sampler) once this is real. Today shell-bun has no Effect dependency, and this would be the reason to take one on.
- **Pause instead of stop** for a child that pushes memory over the budget (SIGSTOP/SIGCONT). It isn't worth doing alone, because a paused process still holds its memory. It only pays with checkpoints that can let memory go.

Priority scheduler: checkpoints that yield and stop, Effect jobs a stop interrupts (#1048)
Closes #1048.

- **`job.checkpoint()`** in `JobContext`. A stopped job throws its `JobStopped` there, so plain JS that calls it actually stops. A low job gives its slot back when a normal job is waiting that would fit in it, or when the sampler has cut low below what's running. It waits at the front of its class for a slot, still holding its memory, so its way back in claims none. `stats().parked` counts these jobs. A stop while parked rejects the checkpoint and doesn't count the slot twice.

title: Priority scheduler: pause over the memory budget, checkpoint(release), parked time off the clock (#1065)
text:
Priority scheduler: pause a child over the memory budget, and scheduler internals on Effect (after #1048)
Carried over from #1048, which added checkpoints (\`job.checkpoint()\`) and \`scheduler.runEffect()\`, an Effect job that a stop interrupts.

- **Pause instead of stop** for a child that pushes memory over the budget (SIGSTOP/SIGCONT). It only pays off once a checkpoint can let memory go: a parked job holds what it has today. One way: a \`release\` hook on the checkpoint, so a job can drop caches or spill to disk before it parks, and the scheduler counts it at its new size.
- **Internals on Effect.** The queue, slots and memory admission are still plain callbacks. Semaphores per class don't fit memory admission or the front-of-queue requeue as they are. The sampler on \`Schedule\` needs a timer that doesn't keep the process alive (today's \`setInterval\` is \`unref\`'d). Worth doing once something inside the scheduler needs an Effect, not for its own sake.
- **Parked time counts toward \`timeoutMs\`.** A low job that keeps stepping aside can time out on wall-clock time. Decide whether parked time should pause the clock.
Priority scheduler: pause over the memory budget, checkpoint(release), parked time off the clock (#1065)
Closes #1065.

The three items in the issue:

- **Pause instead of stop.** With `pause: true`, a job that pushes background work over the memory budget has its tracked process trees stopped with SIGSTOP instead of being put out. It gives its slot back, waits at the front of its class, and gets SIGCONT once it fits again. The kernel can page out a paused child, and each sample counts it at its measured size. If a paused job is stopped (for example by `maxMb`), it gets SIGCONT first so the SIGTERM can land. There's no SIGSTOP on Windows, so there it's put out as before.

text:
codeSplitter: agent budgets per path, hand off to fresh eyes with a caveman-terse note
Agents get worse per dollar as their context grows. Every turn re-reads the whole session, and long sessions also drift. codeSplitter already runs agents (conflict agent, self-heal fix tasks, agent sandbox) and has a per-path policy table (#1050, #1051). Give that table a budget, and have agents hand off to fresh eyes instead of grinding on.

## What to build

1. **Budget columns in the per-path policy table:** a context or spend threshold per task, plus what happens when it's crossed: `handoff` (fresh agent), `escalate` (person), or `downshift` (a cheaper model for mechanical work such as merges, renames and retitles).
2. **Triggers** that cut a run short before the budget runs out:
   - context past the threshold (transcript size; for Claude Code harnesses, a hook can read it)
   - the same failure twice (the same test, or the same error text)
   - a third conflict round on one branch
3. **A handoff note, written caveman-terse.** The next agent reads it cold, so it should be short and blunt:
   ```
   DONE: x, y
   NEXT: z (file:line)
   BROKE: test foo, why
   DONT: tried a, failed because b
   ```

title: codeSplitter mirror branches: carry a file too big to dig, hold a blob main changed too
text:
codeSplitter: a mirror branch skips a file too big to dig, so its merge drops that change
Found replaying PR #1066 through a pull-only mirror (see the dogfood issue).

**What happens:** opening an upstream branch (`POST /api/repos/:o/:r/mirror/branches {ref}`) or pulling one, `take()` in `src/mirror.ts` reads each changed file. A text file over the dig limits (`MAX_BYTES` 256 KB or `MAX_LINES` 5000, `archive.ts`) fails `materializeOn` with a 413 and lands in `skipped`. The only place that shows is a toast when the branch opens. The branch has no row for the file, so the review doesn't list it and the merge lands without it.

**Replay:** #1066 (`office/byte-0943`) added a line to `bun.lock` (431 KB). The branch opened with `skipped: ["bun.lock"]`, and merging it would have shipped the PR without its lockfile change. Git took that change cleanly.

**Expected:** carry it the way a binary file is already carried (#446): as its git blob, shown in the review and written into main's git on merge.

Fixed in the linked PR.

codeSplitter: merging a branch's binary file overwrites main's change to it
Found reading the merge path during the merge dogfood. None of the replays hit it.

**What happens:** `mergeBranch` in `src/branches.ts` treats a branch file held as a git blob (a binary file from a mirror branch, #446) as one that never conflicts. `blobOnMain` writes the branch's blob over main's without looking at main. If main changed the same file after the branch left it, main's change is silently dropped.

**Repro:** a mirror with `logo.bin` on main. Upstream's branch changes `logo.bin`, and the branch opens here. Then upstream's main changes `logo.bin` too, and the mirror syncs. Merging the branch here: main ends up with the branch's bytes, and main's change is only in git history.

**Expected:** if main's blob moved since the branch's fork point (and isn't the branch's blob), hold the merge with a 409 naming the file. Bringing main into the branch upstream and pulling then lets it through. A whole-file pick ("take main's / take the branch's") would be the nicer follow-up.

The linked PR adds the 409 guard. It matters more now that files too big to dig also travel as blobs.

The queue, slots and memory admission are callbacks. Moving them to Effect is worth it only once something inside the scheduler needs an Effect, not for its own sake. Notes for when it does:

- A semaphore per class doesn't fit memory admission (a job's size, an idle worker let go to make room) or the front-of-queue requeue and park as they are.
- The sampler on `Schedule` needs a timer that doesn't keep the process alive (today's `setInterval` is `unref`'d).
- The park/pause waiters (`Waiting.self`) and the stopping clock are the parts a fiber model would replace.
Priority scheduler: checkpoints are Effects, so a stop interrupts a release (#1079)
Closes #1079.

#1079 said to move the scheduler's internals to Effect only once something inside needed one. Something did. `runEffect`'s `checkpointWith(release)` ran the release in a separate `Effect.runPromise`, outside the job's fiber. So when a stop (timeout, memory, eviction) came while the release was running, the release kept going and its finalizers never ran. That broke `runEffect`'s promise that "nothing of it runs on outside the budget".

title: codeSplitter: check an auto-settled merge with the repo's tests, not just the lint (#1096)
text:
codeSplitter: check an auto-settled merge with typecheck/tests, not just the lint
Found replaying PR #1081 through a pull-only mirror (see the dogfood issue).

**What happens:** the line-id merge settled `apps/two-fronts/test/rules.test.ts` with no card, and kept both sides' lines. But the branch renamed the factions (`concord`/`hegemony` → `marines`/`wooka`), and main's side added a new test block that still uses the old names. The settled file would fail typecheck and the test. The person who did the merge by hand renamed main's new lines too. The merge lint (`lint.ts`) caught a similar break in `view.ts` (an undefined identifier), but not a stale object key or string, which only a typecheck or the tests see.

**Missing piece:** the `ci` leftover route only runs for lockfiles. An auto-settled code file has no check beyond the lint. One option: a per-path policy, or a repo setting, that runs the repo's typecheck/tests on the merged tree in a throwaway clone (as `suggest_resolution` and the conflict agent already do) before an auto-settled merge counts as settled. When it fails, the file goes back as a card.

Git did no better here (it conflicted on the file), so this is about how far "auto-settled" can be trusted, not a regression.

codeSplitter: check an auto-settled merge with the repo's tests, not just the lint (#1096)
Closes #1096.

A merge that settled with no card was only checked by the lint (`lint.ts`). The lint can't see a key or string that one side renamed while the other side still uses the old name. That's what happened to #1081's `rules.test.ts`.

- **Policy** (`src/policy.ts`): a new per-path `check: lint | tests`, set in `.gitattributes` with `codesplitter-check=…`. Code defaults to `tests`; lockfiles, config and prose default to `lint`.
- **Merge** (`src/branches.ts`, `testedMerge`): once the dry run has nothing left to settle, each file both sides changed since the fork, under a `tests` policy

title: init: say when a Jekyll site leans on GitHub Pages' other default plugins
text:
Jekyll on GitHub Pages: the other default plugins (optional front matter, relative links, titles from headings)
`rustybuns init` on a Gemfile-less Jekyll repo now copies GitHub Pages' default layouts (jekyll-default-layout) into `_config.rustybuns.yml`. Pages also runs a few other default plugins that plain Jekyll lacks, and a site that leans on them builds differently under Rusty Buns:

- **jekyll-optional-front-matter**: a `.md` with no front matter is rendered as a page on Pages, but copied raw by plain Jekyll.
- **jekyll-relative-links**: `[x](other.md)` links are rewritten to `other.html` on Pages, and left as `.md` links (a 404) otherwise.
- **jekyll-titles-from-headings**: a page with no `title` takes its first heading on Pages.
- **jekyll-readme-index**: a `README.md` serves as the index when there's no `index.md`.

michilotl-studios-docs didn't need these, but plenty of Pages repos do. One option is to have init write a Gemfile with `github-pages` (heavy: the build then needs `bundle install`). Another is to list these plugins in the layer, which needs them installed. Either way, `init` should at least say when a site looks like it depends on them.

title: Two Fronts: the AI plays both sides of the symmetric map the same (#1086)
text:
Two Fronts: the AI wins as the Marines 3 times in 4 on the symmetric full map
Found while pacing the full-campaign galaxy (#1082). The full map is point-symmetric: every world, lane and starting army has a twin on the other side, and `test/rules.test.ts` checks that. Yet in AI-vs-AI wars (seeds 1-60, both sides on `aiOrders`), the Thunder Marines win 46 and the Wooka 14.

Swapping the order of the two `Orders` passed to `resolveTurn` changes nothing, so the bias is inside the engine or the AI. Likely suspects are iteration order (`Object.values(c.systems)` lists the Marine worlds first, and the AI's attack loop takes targets first come, first served) and tie-breaks that favour `marines` in `resolveTurn` and `upkeep` (e.g. `s.orbit = s.fleets.marines ? "marines" : ...`, `for (const f of FACTIONS)`).

To reproduce: run 60 seeds of `newCampaign(seed, "marines", "full")` to a winner and count who wins.

Worth fixing before tuning the full map's difficulty against a human.
Two Fronts: the AI plays both sides of the symmetric map the same (#1086)
Closes #1086.

**Cause.** \`aiOrders\` walked systems in the galaxy's listing order (\`Object.values(c.systems)\`), which starts at the Marines' home worlds. Every first-come choice therefore went differently for each side: where it built, which target a fleet took, and which neighbour won a tie. I found no faction bias in the engine itself. The \`marines\` tie-breaks in \`resolveTurn\` only run once a battle has left one side in the orbit.

**Fix.** The full map lists its systems in twin order (the last is the first one's twin). Each side now reads that list from its own end and sorts neighbo

title: excalibrawl: make the referee test deterministic (#1111)
text:
excalibrawl: Clef referee test is flaky (scores swap when the two sides are judged concurrently)
\`apps/excalibrawl/test/engine.test.ts\` "Clef the referee > scores each side once from its own half, and names the winner" failed on #1107 (a desktop-host 404 change that doesn't touch excalibrawl): run https://github.com/QuinnsCode/RustyBuns/actions/runs/38306949839.

The mock \`run\` hands out likeness scores by call order (\`n++ ? 3 : 1\`), but \`judgeMatch\` judges both sides concurrently. Whichever side's render finishes first gets the 1, so \`m.scores\` sometimes comes back \`[{likeness: 3}, {likeness: 1}]\` and the winner flips.

Fix: score by the side in the call's input (e.g. key on the image or the side name), not by call order. Or, if judging should be ordered, make \`judgeMatch\` deterministic about the order it stores scores.

Closes #1111.

The \"Clef the referee\" test's mock \`run\` handed out likeness scores by call order (\`n++ ? 3 : 1\`). \`judgeMatch\` judges both sides concurrently, so which call came first depended on how long each side's PNG took to encode, and the scores sometimes swapped. That's why it failed CI on #1107 and #1124.

The mock now renders each side's expected snapshot with \`snapshot(scene, regionOf(m, side))\` and scores a call by which of those images it carries (side 0 → 1, side 1 → 3). The test also asserts the two halves really differ, and an image matching neither half scores NaN and

title: Postgres: a hyperdrive binding with the URL as its local twin (#1067)
text:
Postgres / Hyperdrive storage binding with a local twin
Rusty Buns' storage primitive covers D1, KV, R2 and Durable Object storage. It has no Postgres binding. Apps on Supabase, Neon or RDS that query Postgres directly (Drizzle, Prisma, raw SQL) need a Cloudflare Hyperdrive on the Worker, and Rusty Buns can't declare one yet.

What's needed:
- A `hyperdrive` / Postgres binding in `rustybuns.config.ts`. It goes to `Cloudflare.Hyperdrive` (Alchemy v2 already has it, including `Neon.Branch` origins).
- A local twin for desktop and box: pass a `DATABASE_URL` straight through, or run an embedded Postgres (PGlite) for offline use.
- `init` detects `pg` / `postgres` / Drizzle-pg / Prisma-pg and offers the binding.

This is the main gap for bringing Supabase apps in as they are (path A in `notes/SUPABASE.md`), and for the Neon + Hyperdrive exit off Supabase (path B).

```ts
bindings: {
  DATABASE_URL: { type: "secret", op: "op://vault/app/DATABASE_URL" },
  HYPERDRIVE: { type: "hyperdrive", urlSecret: "DATABASE_URL" },   // + configName, caching
}
// app: new pg.Client(env.HYPERDRIVE.connectionString)
```

title: hostScheduler: let a host keep warm workers (RB_WARM, desktop.warm) (#1132)
text:
hostScheduler: let a host app keep warm workers (auto-rig rigs ~2x faster warm)
`hostScheduler()` is made with `warm: 0`, and nothing lets a host app change that. After #1060, auto-rig's TypeScript rigger runs through `hostScheduler().worker("high", ...)`, and a warm worker would roughly halve a rig.

Measured on a Mac (gingerbread mesh, the bundled `src-rig-worker.js`, median of 20 runs after 10 to warm up):

| | rig | overhead per job |
|---|---|---|
| `warm: 0` | 148 ms | 3.4 ms |
| `warm: 1` | 73 ms | 0.36 ms |

The startup overhead is small. Most of the win is that a warm worker keeps `analyze()` JIT-compiled, while a cold one starts from scratch every rig.

Options: an `RB_WARM` env next to `RB_PERSONA`, a `targets.desktop` / box setting baked into the host, or let the first `hostScheduler()` caller pass it. Each idle worker counts `workerMb` against the memory budget, so the default should stay 0.

hostScheduler: let a host keep warm workers (RB_WARM, desktop.warm) (#1132)
Closes #1132.

`hostScheduler()` was always made with `warm: 0`. Now a host app can change that:

- **`targets.desktop.warm`** bakes it into the generated host (`process.env.RB_WARM ||= "n"`), on both the desktop and the box host, the same way a box's `persona` bakes `RB_PERSONA`. `RB_WARM` still overrides it.
- **auto-rig** sets `warm: 1`, so its TypeScript rigger stays loaded between rigs. The issue measured 148 ms cold vs 73 ms warm.

text:

Follow-up to #1067. The `hyperdrive` binding's local twin hands the desktop and box the origin's own `postgres://` URL. With no URL set, the binding is left out, so an offline desktop build has no Postgres.

- Migrations: Drizzle/Prisma migrate against it at boot, the way D1 migrations apply.

`{ type: "hyperdrive", urlSecret: "DATABASE_URL", local: "pglite", migrationsDir: "drizzle" }`: off the edge, when `DATABASE_URL` is unset (an offline desktop), the host starts [PGlite](https://pglite.dev) in `<dataDir>/pglite/<NAME>` and serves it over the Postgres wire protocol on a free 127.0.0.1 port. `env.NAME.connectionString` points there, so `pg`, `postgres` and Drizzle connect unchanged. title: PGlite twin: pooled connections keep their own prepared statements (#1145)
text:
PGlite twin: named prepared statements collide across pooled connections
Follow-up to #1138. The PGlite twin is one Postgres session behind `@electric-sql/pglite-socket`, which queues every connection's queries into it. Named prepared statements from two pooled connections therefore collide (`prepared statement "..." already exists`, 42P05).

Today the docs say: `pg` (unnamed statements by default) works with a Pool; `postgres` and `Bun.SQL` need `prepare: false` (or `max: 1`) against the twin. That's a code difference between the desktop and the edge, which Hyperdrive doesn't need.

Options:
- Rewrite Parse/Bind/Close statement names per connection in the socket layer (prefix with the handler id).
- Or DEALLOCATE a connection's statements when it detaches and treat a duplicate Parse of the same SQL as a no-op.

Repro: `packages/shell-bun/test/pglite.test.ts` with `prepare: false` removed.

PGlite twin: pooled connections keep their own prepared statements (#1145)
Closes #1145.

The PGlite twin is one Postgres session behind `@electric-sql/pglite-socket`. Because of that, named prepared statements from two pooled connections collided (`prepared statement "..." already exists`, 42P05), and `postgres` and `Bun.SQL` needed `prepare: false` on the desktop but not on the edge.

**Fix:** `SessionQueue` in `packages/shell-bun/src/bindings/pglite.ts` replaces pglite-socket's query queue. It has the same three methods its handlers call, and it's installed on the server before `start()`.

title: codeSplitter merge: carry one side's rename into the other side's new lines (#1156)
text:
codeSplitter merge: carry one side's rename into the other side's new lines
The #1096 class came up again in today's replay (#1143). In `apps/two-fronts/test/rules.test.ts`, main renamed `hero` → `heroes`, and #1100's new test lines still used `hero`. codeSplitter settled the file silently, without applying main's rename to the branch's new lines. #1109 now runs the tests on an auto-settled merge, so this gets caught, but caught is not settled: it still goes to an agent.

Proposed: when one side renames an identifier across the file (the existing rename guard already detects this), and the other side's added lines use the old name, apply the rename to those added lines as part of the merge. Then let #1109's test check confirm it.

Limits: only whole-word identifiers the guard has already classed as a rename, and only in lines the other side added. Prose keeps the stopword rules (L2b). If the old name is still defined on main (no real rename), do nothing.

Done when replaying #1100's merge-main fix (401eeda via scripts/merge-replay.ts) settles rules.test.ts exactly like the human fix.

- in a line that side changed, exactly one word became a name or a dotted path (`.hero` → `.heroes.marines`);

title: codeSplitter merge plan: the open branches in waves, by its own merge (#1155)
text:
codeSplitter merge plan: compute merge waves across open branches and auto-update the ones that clash
Today the PR agent did this by hand across about 40 PRs:

1. For each pair of open PRs, dry-run "merge A, then B" (`git merge-tree` on a temp commit) to see which pairs clash.

title: PGlite twin: COPY FROM STDIN and SQL PREPARE/DEALLOCATE ALL per connection (#1150)
text:
PGlite twin: COPY and SQL-level PREPARE/DEALLOCATE ALL still share one session
Follow-up to #1145. SessionQueue (packages/shell-bun/src/bindings/pglite.ts) keeps protocol-level prepared statements apart per pooled connection and holds a connection's turn until its Sync or the end of its transaction. Two cases still act on the shared session:

- `COPY ... FROM STDIN` over a simple query: the turn ends after the Query message, so another connection's messages can land between its CopyData messages. Fix: keep the turn while the backend is in copy-in (watch for CopyInResponse in the output, release on CopyDone/CopyFail).
- SQL `PREPARE name` / `EXECUTE` / `DEALLOCATE ALL`: no prefixing, so names collide and `DEALLOCATE ALL` drops other connections' statements.

Neither showed up with pg, postgres or Bun.SQL defaults. Drizzle/Prisma migrations run through PGlite directly, not over the socket.
PGlite twin: COPY FROM STDIN and SQL PREPARE/DEALLOCATE ALL per connection (#1150)
Closes #1150. Follow-up to #1151 (now on main).

**COPY ... FROM STDIN.** This was worse than the issue said: over the socket it didn't just interleave, it killed the twin. PGlite reads one message's input to the end, so after sending CopyInResponse it hit EOF, logged `FATAL: terminating connection because protocol synchronization was lost`, and the wasm exited, hanging every connection. Now `SessionQueue`:
- answers a lone COPY FROM STDIN query with its own CopyInResponse (text or binary, column count 0, which clients don't read),
- holds the CopyData until CopyDone or CopyFail, touching no s

title: lifecycle tests: wait for the child's pid and SIGINT handler, not fixed sleeps (#1160)
text:
cli: lifecycle SIGTERM deploy test is flaky in CI
`packages/cli/test/lifecycle.test.ts` "deploy stopped by SIGTERM: alchemy finishes its write and exits, the lock is freed" has failed on two PRs that don't touch deploy lifecycle code:

- #1144 (hostScheduler warm workers): run https://github.com/QuinnsCode/RustyBuns/actions/runs/38313827843
- #1157 (build desktop --sign / --notarize): run https://github.com/QuinnsCode/RustyBuns/actions/runs/38316978194

The failure is `expect(received).toBe(expected)` after about 274 ms, so it's probably a race between the signal, alchemy's write and the lock release on a busy CI runner. Every PR that touches `packages/` runs it, so each flake reruns the full suite.

Fix: wait on the event (the child's exit and the lock file's removal) instead of a fixed delay, or give the test its own timeout per the repo's `bun test` timeout quirk. Show it's stable by looping it (e.g. 30 runs) under load (`--parallel` alongside the rest of packages/cli).

lifecycle tests: wait for the child's pid and SIGINT handler, not fixed sleeps (#1160)
Closes #1160.

## Why it flaked

The CI failure was `expect(alive(child)).toBe(false)` getting `true` in a run of normal length (274 ms, vs 277 ms for a pass). It was a test bug, not a lifecycle bug:

- The test polled for `alchemy.pid` to **exist**, then read it. `writeFileSync` creates the file before writing to it, so the read could return `""`.
- `Number("")` is `0`, and `process.kill(0, 0)` signals the test's own process group, so it always succeeds. `alive(0)` is `true`.

title: codeSplitter: a mirror branch that clashes with main only in git takes main in and pushes it (#1190)
text:
codeSplitter: push the line-id merge upstream for mirror branches that clash only in git
Follow-up from #1162.

After a merge, the branches that take main in by themselves are the ones the merge plan says clash: codeSplitter's own merge leaves them a card. A mirror branch whose PR clashes **only in git** isn't one of them. codeSplitter settles it by line id, so its merge here is clean. But upstream, GitHub's PR still shows a conflict until someone brings main in by hand. That's the 3 replays in `bun scripts/merge-plan.ts` that codeSplitter settles by itself (#1110, #1119, #1124).

`pushBranch(..., { tookMain: true })` can already push that settled merge (main's tip plus the branch's copies, as a merge commit). What's missing is the trigger: after a merge, find each open branch with an `upstream_ref` that shares a file with the merged one, check whether `git merge-tree` of its upstream tip and main's new tip clashes, and if so take main in and push.

It needs main's git to hold the merge first. Today git hears about a merge at the next commit of main, so the trigger probably belongs after that commit, not inside the merge.

codeSplitter: a mirror branch that clashes with main only in git takes main in and pushes it (#1190)
Closes #1190.

A mirror branch whose PR clashes with main **only in git** (codeSplitter's line-id merge settles it) now takes main in and pushes the merge upstream on its own, so GitHub's PR stops showing a conflict.

**Trigger:** the mirror's sync, in `followBranches`, which runs after main's commit (and the merge in it) has gone up. For each open branch with an `upstream_ref`, `clashOnlyInGit` runs `git merge-tree` on the branch's upstream tip and main's tip. If git clashes, `takeMainUpstream` runs:
- It skips branches still waiting in the merge plan (`afterBlocker` handles those when their

title: codeSplitter merge: a branch stacked on a squash-merged parent takes only its own changes (#1200)
text:
codeSplitter merge: a branch stacked on a squash-merged parent replays the parent's commits as conflicts
**Seen on #1182.** Its branch (office/nibble-5fef) merged office/pixel-a94d (#1169) in, then #1169 was squash-merged to main as 7466894. Merging main into #1182 now gives 12 conflicts, including add/add on `packages/shell-bun/src/app-server.ts` and `packages/cli/test/app-server.test.ts`, though #1182's own change (#1175) is one commit on top of #1169's (`git diff 4db4895 11a58f3`).

Git sees #1169's work twice: once as the squash on main and once as the original commits on the branch. A merge engine has what it needs to drop that duplicate:

- Detect it: a commit on the branch (or a merged-in parent branch) whose PR has merged, and whose tree diff matches a squash commit on main (same PR number in the subject, or patch-id equality of the combined diff).
- Re-base the merge on that squash: use the parent's last head as the merge base for those files (in effect `git rebase --onto origin/main <parent head>`, written as a merge so nobody force-pushes), so only #1175's lines are left to merge.
- In the merge plan, list stacked branches whose parent merged as "re-base on squash", their own wave, not "conflicting".

Related: #1162 / #1191 (take main in once the blocker merges) covers the 
codeSplitter merge: a branch stacked on a squash-merged parent takes only its own changes (#1200)
Closes #1200.

When a branch upstream is stacked on a parent that main later took in as a squash, git sees the parent's work twice. codeSplitter's mirror now picks the parent's last head as the branch's fork point (`src/mirror.ts` `forkPoint` → `squashedUnder`). That head is the newest commit on the branch whose changes one of main's commits since the merge base already has: the same text, or main's other changes laid on it give main's text (sync.ts `merge3`). Because the check runs against every main commit, it still matches when main edits the parent's files again after the squash, as in #11

title: init: carry over workflows, vectorize, worker loaders, analytics engine, containers, routes, observability and dead-letter queues (#1195)
text:
init: carry over workflows, vectorize, worker_loaders, analytics_engine_datasets, containers, routes, env.* and queue dead-letter queues

Found while trialling init/plan on a real app; see the PR that links this.

title: cli: 30s default timeout for the init and glue tests that spawn the CLI (#1178)
text:
cli: init and deploy-guardrail tests hit bun's default 5s timeout under --parallel load
Found while checking #1160's fix (#1177) by looping `bun test --parallel test/` in `packages/cli` 30 times on macOS and on Linux (Docker, bun 1.4.3). With both loops on the same machine, these tests sometimes ran past bun's default 5 s timeout:

- `test/glue.test.ts`: "deploy guardrail: refuses without a matching plan, accepts --yes" (most often)
- `test/init.test.ts`: "init: refuses to overwrite an existing config unless --force", "init: no package.json, unknown framework and monorepo roots are refused before writing", "init: Astro with @astrojs/cloudflare runs the adapter's Worker, on the desktop too"

Each one spawns the CLI, which takes several seconds under load, and has no timeout of its own. bun 1.4 ignores bunfig's `[test] timeout`, so these get the 5 s default. None of them has failed in CI yet, but they're the next most likely flakes.

Fix: give each one a timeout of its own (like the lifecycle deploy test's `30_000`), or call `setDefaultTimeout` at the top of those files. Then loop them under `--parallel` to confirm.

cli: 30s default timeout for the init and glue tests that spawn the CLI (#1178)
Closes #1178.

`test/init.test.ts` and `test/glue.test.ts` spawn the real CLI, which can take seconds under `--parallel` load, and bun 1.4 ignores bunfig's `[test] timeout`, so they ran on the 5 s default. Both files now call `setDefaultTimeout(30_000)` at the top, the same as `app-server.test.ts`. That covers every spawning test in them, not only the four the issue names.

**Verified:** 5 rounds of two `bun test --parallel test/` runs at once in `packages/cli` on macOS: 243 pass, 0 fail, 0 timeouts in all 10 runs.

title: git-recon battles: lag-compensated hits and input replay (#1181)
text:
git-recon battles: lag-compensated hits and input replay
Follow-up to #1172. Battles' shots are server-authoritative projectiles fired at the shooter's aim point, but the page draws everyone else 100 ms behind (`INTERP` in `apps/git-recon/src/net/mirror.ts`), so at range you lead a target by your latency plus that delay.

- Rewind targets by the shooter's latency when a round from a player is checked against soldiers (each soldier already keeps a `trail`; it'd need finer samples than `TRAIL_EVERY` = 0.25 s).
- Replace the soft position correction for your own soldier with input sequence numbers and replay, so a correction doesn't fight a fast strafe.

Measure on a real LAN first: it may not matter at LAN latencies.

git-recon battles: lag-compensated hits and input replay (#1181)
Closes #1181.

## Lag-compensated hits
- Each input the page sends now carries `view`: the battle time it drew everyone else at (its clock minus `INTERP`). - In a battle, the world records every soldier's position and body height each tick (120 Hz) for the last 0.3 s. That's finer than the 0.25 s `trail`, which revert still uses.
- A player's round carries `rewind` = their lag, and `soldierAt` checks it

title: CI: kill a hung test run after 10 min and name the file
text:
CI: a hung test run should fail fast and name the file, not sit until the job timeout
**Seen on #1199.** `test codesplitter` sat in `bun ../../scripts/ci-test-count.ts "bun test --parallel test"` for 10+ minutes (normally ~1 min, run 38327564716) until it was cancelled by hand. Bun's per-test timeout doesn't catch a deadlock in shared setup or an event loop that never drains, and the job's timeout-minutes is 30, so a PR sits "pending" with no clue which file hangs. The cause was probably #1199's Durable Object gate change (`turn()` plus the RPC Proxy in packages/shell-bun) deadlocking a codeSplitter test.

The fix belongs in `scripts/ci-test-count.ts`, which every app's test step already runs through:
- Give the whole command a wall-clock budget: a few times the app's usual duration, or a `--budget` flag set per app in `scripts/ci-apps.ts`.
- When the budget runs out, print the test files that started but never finished (from bun's output as it streams), kill the process tree, and exit non-zero with `::error title=hung::<file>`.
- The office PR board, and codeSplitter's CiRunner/merge plan, can then show "hung in X" in place of an endless pending.

This matters for the merge engine too: a settled merge whose tests hang currently looks the same as tests still running

text:
git-recon battles: raise the 32-player cap now snapshots are deltas
Follow-up to #1183. With snapshots as binary deltas, a room past 32 players is cheap on CPU; bandwidth is now what decides it.

Measured on el-capitan, teams, half the players walking and a third firing (the `tests/battle.test.ts` 32-player setup), 40 ticks, joining past `MAX_PLAYERS` by hand:

| players | step ms/tick | snapshots ms/tick | bytes a player a snapshot | out of the room |
|--|--|--|--|--|
| 32 | 1.4–2.0 | 1.6–2.2 | 855 | ~535 KB/s |
| 48 | 2.2 | 3.4 | 1137 | ~1.0 MB/s |
| 64 | 2.8 | 5.4 | 1463 | ~1.8 MB/s |

A tick has 50 ms, so 64 fits on CPU. 64 costs what 32 did before #1183.

- What's left in a delta: about a third is events, ~130 B is your own ammo/cooldowns as JSON (changes every tick while firing). Binary for `you` and a lighter event encoding would be the next cut.

Two gaps:

1. **Dispatch the rebuild.** When the merge plan sees a branch whose blocker merged and the clash is real, start an agent with the rebuild-pr recipe (merge main, regenerate generated files, run the narrow tests, push), in place of only flagging it. codeSplitter rebuild task: push upstream when it finishes, and collect its ENGINE lines
Follow-up to #1219.

A rebuild task (`rebuildOnMain` in `apps/codesplitter/src/branches.ts`) now restarts a really-clashing branch from main's copies and has an agent put main's side back. Two things it doesn't do yet:

title: codeSplitter merge: a sentence both sides edited merges word by word, unless a changed number is quoted (#1222)
text:
codeSplitter merge: word-level merge inside a sentence both sides edited
**Seen on #1221** (git-recon 64 players) against main after #1205 (battles online). `apps/git-recon/README.md` line 4, one sentence:

- base: "…or by up to **32** players in one battle that the desktop app hosts in its world and opens to the LAN."
- main (#1205): "…up to 32 players … opens to the LAN**, or online in a Durable Object per room**."
- PR: "…up to **64** players … opens to the LAN."

The two edits are disjoint words. L3 splits prose into sentences and merges *whole* sentences, so when both sides touch the same sentence it's a card. The same thing happens in the `src/net/room.ts` bullet: main added a sentence after it, and the PR rewrote numbers inside it.

Proposal, L3c: when a paired sentence was edited on both sides, diff3 it at word level (tokens = words + punctuation). Settle it when the changed word ranges don't overlap or touch. Otherwise it stays a card. Guard: refuse if one side's change is a number and the other side's text quotes that number elsewhere in the paragraph (the "32-player test" mentions in the room.ts bullet are deliberately left at 32).

This is the most common git-recon README clash: every battles PR this round (#1205, #1208, #1214, #1221) hit RE

Closes #1222.

**What I found.** The engine already does what the issue asks for. A line both sides changed goes through `mergeWords`, a word-level diff3 that settles when the changed spans don't overlap or touch. The sentence-level L3 split only applies inside stretches both sides reshaped. title: PGlite twin: DISCARD ALL stays per connection, DISCARD TEMP refused (#1167)
text:
PGlite twin: DISCARD ALL / DISCARD PLANS still reset the shared session
Follow-up to #1150 (PR #1166). On the PGlite twin every pooled connection shares one Postgres session. #1166 scoped `DEALLOCATE ALL` to the calling connection, but `DISCARD ALL` (pgbouncer's default `server_reset_query`, and what some poolers send on release) still runs as-is. It drops every connection's prepared statements, temp tables, GUCs and advisory locks. `DISCARD PLANS` / `DISCARD TEMP` have a smaller version of the same problem.

Possible fix: in `SessionQueue.rewrite`, turn `DISCARD ALL` into the connection-scoped deallocate DO block plus whatever else is safe to reset per connection, or refuse it with a readable error as COPY-in-a-batch is.

Not seen with pg, postgres or Bun.SQL defaults.

text:
codeSplitter merge: carry a branch's edit into a block main moved (and re-indented)
Found while rebuilding #1210 on main (merge commit 77af4b1, `bun scripts/merge-replay.ts 77af4b1`): git conflicted on `apps/codesplitter/src/mirror.ts` (`followBranches`), and codeSplitter's line-id merge left it as 2 cards.

Both sides reordered the same `if` chain in `followBranches`. Before, it was `if (tip === had) { delete merged branch } else if (open) { catchUp }`.
- main (#1209) put `if (open) { ...; continue }` first and moved the delete-merged block out under it, unindented.
- #1210 put `if (open) { catchUp }` first and the delete block under `else if (tip === had)`, then added one line to it: `update-ref -d squashRef(ref)`.

**Card 2 (L1037) is the gap.** Main moved the delete block and changed its indent, and the branch added one line inside it. The fix is main's moved block plus the branch's line. The line-id merge reads main's move as a delete plus an insert, so it can't carry the branch's line into the moved copy. To fix it: match moved runs by text, ignoring whitespace (as the stacked-branch rebase already matches merged lines by text), and replay the branch's in-run edits onto the moved copy.

title: codeSplitter: fix tasks ride a FIXES queue of their own, not JOBS (#1234)
text:
codeSplitter: rebuild tasks wait behind feature runs in the JOBS queue
Follow-up to #1219 / #1227 (second failure mode in the #1219 comments).

`rebuildOnMain` opens its rebuild through `openFix` (heal.ts), which sends it to `env.JOBS`. That's the same queue as every other agent run (`max_concurrency: 8` in `apps/codesplitter/wrangler.jsonc`). With the slots full of feature runs, a rebuild waits for one to finish, even though rebuilds are short and unblock merges.

Fix: a rebuild (and probably every fix task) gets its own slot or jumps the queue, e.g. a separate queue binding for fix tasks, or a reserved slot the consumer only hands to `agent_runs` rows opened by heal.ts.

title: plan --usage: estimate the fan-out per cron tick and request (#1224)
text:
plan's cost report: estimate the fan-out per cron tick and request, not just list resources
`plan` lists each billable resource with its pricing model (`usage  requests + CPU time`) but no volume. The bill comes from the fan-out: a large real RWSDK app trialled locally has a `* * * * *` cron whose one tick runs ~20 sweeps, and each sweep makes several Durable Object RPCs (rwsdk/db goes through a DO per query), queue sends and sometimes Workers AI calls. That's 1,440 ticks a day × the fan-out, and a DO poked every minute never hibernates, so its duration is billed around the clock.

The desktop host already sees all of this: every cron tick, DO event, queue op and AI call goes through our twins. Proposal:
- [ ] count per binding (DO requests and awake-seconds, queue ops, D1 rows, R2 ops, AI neurons, subrequests) on the desktop host, exposed at `/__rb/mem` or a sibling `/__rb/usage`
- [ ] `plan` turns a run of that into a monthly estimate (per tick × ticks/month, per request × a stated traffic figure), next to the resource list
- [ ] flag crons that keep a DO awake 24/7

Related: COSTS.md.
plan --usage: estimate the fan-out per cron tick and request (#1224)
Closes #1224.

`plan` listed each billable resource with no volume. Now it can also show a monthly estimate built from what a running host's bindings actually did.

**Counting (shell-bun `usage.ts`)**
- Each unit of work runs inside a *cause*: `request`, `cron <expr>` or `queue <binding>` (one run per message). The cause is carried by AsyncLocalStorage, so a DO RPC three awaits deep, or an alarm set during a tick, still counts toward that tick. Work with no cause (socket frames) lands in `other`.
- What gets counted: DO requests, the distinct objects each run touches and how long it holds them

title: codeSplitter merge: one card for a clash split only by lines the other side moved away (#1237)
text:
codeSplitter merge: show one card, not three, for a stretch split only by lines the other side moved away
Follow-up from #1223 / #1236.

A rebuild task (`rebuildOnMain` in `apps/codesplitter/src/branches.ts`) now restarts a really-clashing branch from main's copies and has an agent put main's side back. Two things it doesn't do yet:

title: codeSplitter merge: keep main's line when the branch moved its base line into a card (#1248)
text:
codeSplitter merge: main's line is lost when the branch moved its base line into a card
Found while working on #1237.

In the three-way merge of `apps/codesplitter/src/mirror.ts` (base 6cf4a6a, main 292102d, branch 4893930, each side diffed through `diffToOps`), main's `continue;` at the end of the `if (br.status === "open")` block is lost, even though it sits outside the card.

Why: main's diff gave that `continue;` the id of base's `if (theirs) await catchUp(…)` line. The branch moved that base line up into its rewritten `open` block, which is inside the card. `mergeLines` reads the base line as moved on the branch, so it deletes main's copy (the `movedOnBranch` case in the loop over base lines). The branch's moved copy is in the card, so the loop skips it. Main's `continue;` is gone whatever the pick, `main` included. This also happens before #1237.

To get the hand fix 77af4b1 today, the card's text has to include `continue;`, though main's side of the card doesn't show it.

A fix might be: when a base line's branch move lands inside a clash region, and main has changed that line, don't delete main's line for the move.

Closes #1248.

In a three-way merge, main's diff can give a new line (here `continue;`) the id of a base line (`if (theirs) await catchUp(…)`) that the branch moved into a stretch both sides reshaped. The loop over base lines read that as a branch move, so it deleted main's line, though the line sits outside the card. Main's `continue;` was lost whatever the pick, `main` included.

Now, when the branch moved a base line into a card and main changed that line, main's line stays. The card settles the move.

title: init: warn when a wrangler limits block holds more than cpu_ms (#1258)
text:
init: a wrangler limits block with more than cpu_ms no longer warns (lost in #1199's merge of main)
Found by the merge replay in `apps/codesplitter/docs/merge-solutions.md` §10. This isn't a codeSplitter bug: it's something the hand fix lost.

#1199 (`70702de`, merging main into `office/gizmo-451d`) made `rustybuns init` report a wrangler `limits` block as dropped unless all it held was `cpu_ms`. Its new test:

```ts
// limits.cpu_ms is carried (worker.cpuMs); any other limit is not
expect(droppedWranglerKeys({ limits: { cpu_ms: 30000, subrequests: 100 } } as any)).toEqual(["limits"]);
```

Main (#1212) had put `"limits"` in `HANDLED`. The fix took main's `droppedWranglerKeys` and dropped the branch's clause and test. So today, `init` on a wrangler config with `limits.subrequests` (or any limit other than `cpu_ms`) carries only `cpu_ms` and doesn't warn that the rest was dropped.

Fix: in `packages/cli/src/wrangler.ts`, keep `limits` in `HANDLED` but report it when `Object.keys(w.limits ?? {})` has anything other than `cpu_ms`, and bring back the branch's test in `packages/cli/test/init.test.ts`.

title: codeSplitter merge: flag prose that settled but may now be untrue (#1254)
text:
codeSplitter merge: a paragraph the other side made untrue settles silently (README numbers, caps)
Found by the merge replay of 14 hand-fixed "merge main" commits (`bun apps/codesplitter/scripts/merge-replay.ts …`, written up in `apps/codesplitter/docs/merge-solutions.md` §10). This was the most common miss in that replay: 5 of the 20 files that weren't exact.

**What happens.** One side writes or edits a README paragraph, and the other side changes the facts it states: a number, a cap, a format. The line merge has nothing to clash on, or keeps one side's words, so the file settles with no card. The text is a faithful merge of the two sides, and it's out of date.

|---|---|---|

| #1214 `d7ffea8` | git-recon README | added "and each snapshot echoes the newest input the world had" for the branch's input replay |
| #1189 `137baa3` | git-recon README | "On your own, down 15 guards", "In a battle everyone carries every gun"

text:
codeSplitter merge: a local whose code moved into a new function (`dry` read as `run.dry` after an extract) still cards
Follow-up to #1257.

#1257 scopes `renames()` to a function, so the shape the issue describes (a function whose own lines go from `dry` to `run.dry`) carries into main's new line there. But in the real #1191 commit (`0ebf5e2`, `apps/codesplitter/src/branches.ts`), the branch's `mergeBranch` never has a line that went from `dry` to `run.dry`. The base lines that used `dry` (`for (const d of dry)`, `dry.filter(…)`) moved, by line id, into the new `dryRun()`, and `mergeBranch` only gained `const run = await dryRun(…)`. With nothing left to infer the rename from, main's new `rebuilt(…, dry, user)` line is still a lint card (`` `dry` is not defined ``). That card is safe.

To settle it, the merge would have to read "this code moved into a function that returns `{ dry }`, and its call is assigned to `run`" as `dry` becoming `run.dry` in the caller. That's a much bigger inference, so it may not be worth doing. File it under replay gaps unless it comes up again.

Follow-up to #1219 / #1227 (first failure mode in the #1219 comments).

title: worker-mode host: honour fetch's cf.cacheTtl / cacheEverything with a local cache (#908)
text:
worker-mode host: honour fetch's cf.cacheTtl / cacheEverything with a local cache
On Cloudflare, `fetch(url, { cf: { cacheTtl, cacheEverything } })` is answered from the edge cache. The desktop and box hosts ignore `cf`, so every request makes the real outbound call.

redwoodjs/rwsdk.com's star widget fetches `https://api.github.com/repos/redwoodjs/sdk` with `cf: { cacheTtl: 14400 }` on every render. Under the host, 200 GETs of `/` made 200 GitHub calls and got rate-limited ("abuse detection"). Each failure is logged with `console.error`, and Bun prints the minified source line with it, which took 61% of the CPU. Result: p50 54 ms and p95 242 ms, against 2-5 ms for comparable apps.

Fix: a small in-process (or sqlite) response cache for outbound fetches that set `cf.cacheTtl`, keyed by method and URL and honouring the TTL. This only matters in worker mode.

Found by `scripts/trial-github.ts --dep rwsdk --major 1` (#907).

It follows the edge's rules: GET/HEAD only, keyed by method and URL. `cacheTtl` caches 200/206/301/302/303/404/410 for that many seconds (0 or less means no caching). `cacheEverything` on its own uses the response's `s-m

title: codeSplitter desktop: git in a repo folder that isn't there is a failed run, not a throw (#887)
text:
codeSplitter desktop: digging a big repo 500s, seeGit runs before the local clone exists
On the desktop (local twins), digging a big public GitHub repo fails with a 500 before the repo row is usable:

```
ENOENT: no such file or directory, posix_spawn 'git'
  at git (apps/codesplitter/src/mirror.ts:85)
  at seeGit (apps/codesplitter/src/mirror.ts:564)
  at githubRoutes (apps/codesplitter/src/github.ts:465)
```

**Cause:** `LocalArtifacts.import` (`packages/shell-bun/src/bindings/artifacts.ts:113`) starts `git clone --bare` in the background and returns right away. `POST /api/github/dig` then calls `seeGit`, which runs `git rev-parse` with the bare repo as its cwd. The clone hasn't made that folder yet, so the spawn fails on the missing cwd (reported as `posix_spawn 'git'`). Small repos clone fast enough to dodge it.

**Repro:** `local()` from `src/local.ts`, then `POST /api/github/dig {"repo":"pingdotgg/t3code"}` (105 MB packed at depth 1).

**Fix ideas:** have `seeGit` wait on the import (or skip when the folder isn't there yet and set `git_seen` when the import lands), and make `git()` report a missing cwd as a failed run rather than throwing. Worked around in a scratch script by awaiting `artifacts.importing` inside `import`. With that, the dig landed: a 113 MB bare

title: codeSplitter: revert or cherry-pick a commit that touches a binary file (#888)
text:
codeSplitter: revert or cherry-pick a commit that touches a binary file
Follow-up to #880. Revert and cherry-pick (pick.ts) land a commit's changes as line edits, so a commit that touches a binary or too-big file is refused with a 409 clash ("a binary file: it has no lines to undo or take"). They could write those blobs through catalogueBlob, the way a branch merge does (#446), as long as main's copy still matches the commit's other side.
codeSplitter: revert or cherry-pick a commit that touches a binary file (#888)
Closes #888.

Until now, a revert or cherry-pick of a commit that touched a binary or too-big file was refused with a 409 ("a binary file: it has no lines to undo or take").

**Now, on main:** the file's bytes go into git as they are, in the **same** git commit as the line edits. This is only allowed when main's copy still matches the side the commit goes from, byte for byte. That means the commit's after for a revert, or its before for a pick. title: codeSplitter: revert or cherry-pick a binary file onto an open branch (#1298)
text:
codeSplitter: revert or cherry-pick a binary file onto an open branch
Follow-up to #888 (PR #1297). A revert or pick on main now writes a binary file's bytes into git. On an open branch it still clashes ("a binary file: only main takes those").

A branch holds a binary as a `branch_files.blob` hash, and the merge reads its bytes from the mirror's git (`blobBytes`, #446). That only works when the mirror's git has the blob. To fix it, the branch row could point at the commit's blob (it's in the repo's own git), and `blobOnMain` could read it from there when the mirror doesn't have it.

title: codeSplitter: keep a hosted preview's state sealed until a later destroy succeeds (#1299)
text:
codeSplitter: keep a hosted preview's state sealed until a later destroy succeeds
Split out of #1294, whose CiRunner half is done.

A doctor's preview on the site (#900, `deploy-runner.ts`) keeps no Alchemy state: it goes up and comes down in one container. When its destroy fails, the container goes and takes the state with it, so the `preview-<id>` stack stays up and someone has to take it down by hand in the provider's dashboard (the run's note says so).

Fix: when a hosted preview's destroy fails, seal that stage's state (`sealState`, as deploys do) under a key of its own in the DeployRunner. A later alarm restores it in a fresh container and runs the destroy again, and drops the sealed state only once a destroy succeeds. The test is a fake container whose first destroy fails: the second alarm brings the stack down, and nothing sealed is left after that.

codeSplitter: every API call costs 450-700ms, even /api/me
Measured from Chrome (SJC colo) on the live site, signed in, private repo `quinn/checks-776`:

| request | ms |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/me` | 594 |
| `GET /api/repos/quinn/checks-776/branches` | 476-734 |
| `GET /api/repos/quinn/checks-776/do/file?path=slow.test.ts` | 413-440 |
| `GET /` (page shell, `cf-cache-status: HIT`) | 152 |

The page shell is edge cached. The API isn't, and can't be as is: reads are private and per user. So every call pays the full `route()` preamble in `src/worker.ts` before its handler runs: `identify()` (a D1 session lookup), `limit()` (a rate limit tally), then `record()` for insights. Even a trivial `/api/me` pays all of that, so it's probably several sequential D1 round trips from the edge to D1's primary.

To find out:
- Add `Server-Timing` to API responses (identify / limit / handler) to see where the ~450ms goes.
- Options: cache the session lookup at the edge (Cache API or an in-isolate map keyed by cookie for a few seconds), D1 read replicas (Sessions API) for reads, skip the D1 limit tally on GETs that the edge in-memory count covers.

A file switch fires ~20 of these calls. #1314 removes the client's sequential waits.

codeSplitter tests: make the claim-lapse re-claim test deterministic
Closes #1322.

The test read `Date.now()` before the claim, then jumped to `t0 + LEASE_MS + 1`. When the claim took a while under `--parallel`, its lease started after `t0` and outlasted that jump, so the re-claim got 409. It now reads the clock after the claim lands.

Agent Office queue: Wait holds the task until its busy branches merge
Closes #1287.

The hint card's **Wait** used to drop the task. Now the office server holds it (`/__rb/codesplitter/hold`, in memory, 14 days) with the open branches it waits on. Each time codeSplitter's branch list shows none of them open, the task is ready. An open office page checks on its 30s poll and claims each ready task once (`hold/take`), then sends the `queue.add` on its socket. If codeSplitter can't answer, the task keeps waiting.

## What
`bun native/stress/genome.ts [--native 4] [--wasm 4] [--iters 2000000] [--genes 64]`

title: shell-bun: request limits survive an app that swaps process for unenv's
text:
shell-bun: request limits survive an app that swaps process for unenv's
## What

A worker-mode desktop app built with `nodejs_compat` replaces `globalThis.process` with unenv's, whose `cpuUsage` and `memoryUsage.rss` throw `[unenv] process.cpuUsage is not implemented yet!`. `capped()` in `edge-limits.ts` called them per request, so every request answered 500.

Found running a real RedwoodSDK freight app (D1, Durable Objects, workflows, Vectorize, queues) as a desktop app: it built, started, and 500'd on every page. With this change the page answers 200.

## Fix

Take `process.cpuUsage` and `process.memoryUsage.rss` once at import, before app code runs.

title: rustybuns: protect: true keeps a resource through destroy
text:
rustybuns: protect: true keeps a resource through destroy
## What

`protect: true` on a `d1`, `kv`, `r2`, `queue`, `vectorize` or `hyperdrive` binding makes `destroy` leave that resource and its data on the account. The generated stack decorates it with Alchemy's `RemovalPolicy.retain()`, so the provider's delete is never called.

## UI

`plan`, `deploy` and `destroy` print a block first:

```
protection (destroy):
  [KEPT]    Vectorize shop-index: destroy leaves it, and its data, on the account
  [REMOVED] D1 shop-db: destroy deletes it, and its data
```

In ADOPT mode the destroy prompt lists what it deletes and what it keeps. Stages can override i

title: codeSplitter gitpath: show a file's history from before it was on codeSplitter
text:
codeSplitter gitpath: show a file's history from before it was on codeSplitter
Imports are depth 1, so a dug repo's own git starts at the import and gitpath showed one commit. gitpath is for seeing the code's whole story, so for a repo with a GitHub upstream the commits before the import now come from GitHub's commit API (the file's commits, with line counts for the newest 40) and are joined onto the hosted ones: the import root takes the older commits as its parents. The busiest-files list adds GitHub's latest 30 commits too, so a fresh import has files to pick. If GitHub won't answer (private without a token, rate limit) the hosted history shows as before.

title: agent-office: plan for running the office inside codeSplitter (#1384)
text:
Agent Office inside codeSplitter: preview it ephemerally, then move for real
Make Agent Office run inside codeSplitter, so the office (workers, task queue, PR board) is a codeSplitter feature instead of a separate Bun binary (`apps/agent-office`).

## Why
- One place for PRs, merge waves, the Mervin merge engine and the workers that fix conflicts.
- The office already leans on codeSplitter: the dispatch hint (#1187), the "hung in X" CiRunner annotation (#1218), and the Wait hold on busy branches (#1356).

## The catch
The PR agent that fixes things runs on the office being moved. Moving it for real would cut off the agent that could repair it. So do it in two steps.

## Plan
1. **Ephemeral first.** Deploy the office inside codeSplitter as a separate preview (its own stage, destroyed after verifying; price it first, smallest resources). The current office keeps running and keeps its PR agent. Drive the preview with a throwaway queue and check: hiring a worker, the task queue, the PR board, merge/rebuild flows, worker identity (#942).
2. **List what has to move.** Worker terminals and git worktrees need a real machine or sandbox (AgentSandbox), so work out what stays local and what becomes a codeSplitter service. Write that list on this issue before building.

text:
Thick borg (future): an app per common migration story
**Future plan.** Slim borg checks each primitive once. Thick borg is a decent-sized app per common migration story, run through the same kind of suite on each target. Each app is also the example for its story.

Split the stories by three separate choices (where the code runs, which engine, who hosts the data) and write one adapter per choice, never one per combination.

Stories, most common first:

- [ ] **Keep the database, move the code:** a Node or Next app on Postgres (Neon) moved to a Worker through Hyperdrive, and to a Hetzner box. Needs a `postgres` binding: Hyperdrive on the edge, a direct connection on a box, PGlite as the desktop twin, and a Neon branch per test stack.
- [ ] **Leave a PaaS for a box:** Railway or Heroku to Hetzner, with sqlite or Postgres on the volume
- [ ] **Go all-edge:** Postgres to D1, with a lint that flags what D1 won't run (`BEGIN`, `ATTACH`, too many bound parameters)
- [ ] **Lambda + DynamoDB to Workers + KV / Durable Objects**
- [ ] **Mongo:** probably "keep Atlas, move the code". Check whether FerretDB works as a twin.
- [ ] Better Auth on all three targets: a secret minted per install on desktop, and login handled by the edge with the sessio

title: codeSplitter: protect main from crew and agents
text:
codeSplitter: protect main from crew and agents (branches only, agent batches wait for a person)
Found in the agent lockdown review. A design call for the owner, so not changed in that PR.

**What happens today**

- Any crew member, an invited agent included, can commit straight to `main` with `/do/ops` then `/do/commit`, or with revert/pick (`apps/codesplitter/src/worker.ts:684-766`, `:560-563`). That skips branches, required checks and the build-file review, and with a mirror the commit goes upstream with the owner's credentials (`worker.ts:765`).
- A hosted agent's batch lands on `main` by itself after `AGENT_REVIEW_MS`, 8 seconds by default (`src/agent-routes.ts:129`, `:559-568`). The only holds are build files when deploy-on-commit is on, and required checks when the repo has some.
- Nothing like an approval exists: any crew member merges any branch, its own included (`src/branches.ts:966-970`).

**Proposal**

An owner setting, "protect main". With it on:
1. Crew (people and agents) edit on branches only. Direct ops and commits on `main` are the owner's.
2. Agent batches wait for a person (`until: null`) instead of an 8-second timer.
3. Merging a branch needs someone other than its author to accept it.

On by default for new repos once the demo period is over (after Oct 2

2. An agent's batch always gets its own branch and waits for a person (`until: null`), not the 8-second timer. An agent can't accept its own batch.
3. A branch's author can't merge it.

Found in the agent lockdown review. Smaller gaps, each its own fix.

1. **Crew can start the owner's hosted agents.** A failed required check on any branch opens a heal fix task whose text is the log's tail (`apps/codesplitter/src/checks.ts:180`, `src/heal.ts:140-146,186-198`). Heal checks that the owner is an admin, not who set it off (`heal.ts:44`). Crew merges start conflict agents too (`src/branches.ts:354,505,508`). There are 2 tries per branch but no limit on branches, so crew can use up the site's 30 runs a day (`src/limits.ts:78`). The per-person `agent` limit (`limits.ts:77`) is never charged.
2. **`build_ok` is self-attested.** Any crew member merges a branch that changes build files by sending `build_ok: true` (`src/branches.ts:681`). It should be the owner's word, or someone other than the branch's author.
3. **A read token gets a write remote on the desktop.** `GET /api/repos/:o/:r` hands the owner a day-long write remote to the bare repo (`src/worker.ts:471-472`), so the owner's read-scope token can push to `main` through `landPushes`.
4. **`agent-<harness>` crew rows are never removed** (`src/worker.ts:649`), and queued jobs replay as their user through `actingAs` af

Closes #1429.

- `build_ok` counts only from the owner or someone other than the branch's author (`branches.ts`), so a crew member can't wave through their own build-file change.
- Hosted fix tasks (check failures, guard trips, rebuilds) start only when the branch's author is an admin (`heal.ts openFix`), so crew can't spend the site's runs.

title: codeSplitter: split admin out of write tokens and hold a token to a repo
text:
codeSplitter: a write token or OAuth grant is the whole account; hold it to repos and split out admin
Found in the agent lockdown review.

A personal `cst_` write token, or an OAuth/MCP grant, can do everything its person can on every repo they own, except the cookie-only routes (`apps/codesplitter/src/tokens.ts:40`). That includes:

- deleting a repo or changing its visibility,
- adding or removing crew and minting invites,
- minting CI tokens,
- adding webhooks,
- setting deploy keys,
- changing check settings.

See `src/worker.ts:483,495,644,657`, `src/hooks.ts:207`, `src/gh-compat.ts:45` and `src/checks.ts:721`. The MCP `destructiveHint` is advisory (`src/mcp.ts:13-16`). An agent handed its owner's token, then prompt-injected, has the owner's whole account.

**Proposal**

1. A token or grant can be held to some repos (invite-agent tokens already are, `tokens.ts:74-76`).
2. A third scope between write and the cookie: `write` edits code, branches and checks; `admin` (or cookie only) covers delete, visibility, crew, invites, CI tokens, webhooks, deploy keys and check settings.
3. The consent page and the token page say which one is being handed out.

codeSplitter: split admin out of write tokens and hold a token to a repo
Closes #1427.

- New `admin` token scope. `write` edits code, branches and checks; deleting a repo, visibility, crew, invites, CI tokens, webhooks, deploy keys and check settings (mutations only) now need `admin` or the cookie. Enforced in one place, `adminRoute` in `tokens.ts`.
- OAuth/MCP grants stay read/write, so they are never admin; the consent page says so.
- `POST /api/tokens` takes `repo` (owner/name) to hold a token to one repo, as invite tokens already are. The profile page has the admin option and a repo field.

title: borg: fatty borg, the chunky examples through build, deploy and teardown
text:
Fatty borg (future): build, deploy and teardown the chunky example apps
**Future plan.** Fatty borg runs the chunky example apps through the whole lifecycle, to catch what only shows up at size: build time, binary size, deploy and teardown, and state left behind.

Use apps that already exist rather than building new ones:

- [ ] codeSplitter (queues, Artifacts, many Durable Objects)
- [ ] tscircuit-desktop (a heavy Vite app plus a Rust engine)
- [ ] park-hide-seek (Durable Objects plus big assets)
- [ ] agent-office (PTYs, so desktop and box only)

Each run: `build desktop`, `build box`, `plan`, `deploy` to a throwaway stage, a smoke check, `destroy`, then confirm nothing is left (no stray Workers, D1 databases, buckets or boxes). Record timings and sizes against the last run.

This costs money, so run it on demand or weekly, never on every PR. Price it with `plan` first, cap it, and destroy even when a step fails.

borg: fatty borg, the chunky examples through build, deploy and teardown
Closes #857.

`bun fatty.ts` lists the steps for codeSplitter, tscircuit-desktop, park-hide-seek and agent-office; `--run` does them (on demand, costs money). Edge deploys go to a `fatty<ts>` stage behind the plan cost cap, destroy always runs, a sweeper checks for leftovers, and timings/sizes print against the last green run.

- codeSplitter's deploy is refused until its config has a `stages` entry for fatty runs: it pins the Worker name and adopts, so a throwaway stage would take over the live Worker. Builds and plan still run.

Found while building `bun run smoke` (#1445).

Running the files the security model cites in one `bun test` process, without `--parallel`, fails 7 tests that pass when their file runs alone:

- `codesplitter.test.ts`: the two `levels` import tests (the level sits at `importing`; a push to `level-mitt.git` answers 404), the queued-dig rate limit test (times out), the game backrooms test, and the two private-lines tests (`artifacts.readFile` answers null).

title: codeSplitter: a Durable Object of your own for your settings, light/dark first
text:
codeSplitter: user settings in their own Durable Objects, moved near the user
Per-user settings (light/dark mode, density, last tab, and the like) should live in a Durable Object near the user, not in a central D1 row, so a change is stored close to them everywhere.

**Shape:** one `UserSettings` Durable Object per user, SQLite-backed, created with a location hint from where they first connect. The Worker reads and writes it by user id. localStorage stays as the instant paint; the DO is the source of truth across devices.

**Movement:** track coarse location (the `cf.colo`/country on each request, no precise location). When a user is consistently served from somewhere far from their DO, move it. Durable Objects can't migrate by themselves, so the move is: create a new DO with a hint at the new region, copy the settings, point the user at it, delete the old one. Needs a threshold (for example 5 requests in a row from the new region over a day) so a trip doesn't churn.

**Open questions:** where the id to DO mapping lives (a small D1 row, or deterministic `idFromName` with the region in the name); whether the move is worth it for a few KB of settings (price it before building); privacy page wording for the location signal ([#privacy](apps/codesplitter/src/priv

title: Mervin board --score: count rebuilt PRs that merged as landed
text:
Mervin board --score: a PR rebuilt after the board ran counts as not landed
On 2026-10-13 a board ran over 30 open PRs (main 1450913c). During the merge round, 11 of them merged (#1432, #1442, #1455, #1457, #1458, #1462, #1476, #1486, #1495, #1499, #1459/#1461). Most had been rebuilt first, by merging main in, which gave them new head commits. Then `bun scripts/mervin-board.ts --score <dir> --main origin/main` reported:

```
sandbox from 1450913ca vs main c9bc3f515: 0 of 30 PRs landed
  moved 94   waiting 32
```

It looks like the score matches each PR by the head sha the board recorded (not confirmed). A merge round always rebuilds PRs, so the score can never see the PRs it's meant to grade.

**Fix:** find a landed PR by its number: the `Merge pull request #N` or `(#N)` commit on main's first-parent history, or `gh pr view N --json state,mergeCommit`. Then compare each file's text on main against the sandbox's copy for that PR.

**Test:** a PR whose branch gets a new commit after the board ran, then merges. The score must count it as landed and grade its files.

Part of #1526.
Mervin board --score: count rebuilt PRs that merged as landed
Closes #1530

`--score` now walks main's first-parent history and recognises a landed PR by its number (`Merge pull request #N` or `(#N)`), so rebuilding a PR after the board ran no longer hides it. Walking first-parent also stops a merged branch's own commits from marking its files `moved`.

Test: a PR gets a new head commit after the board ran, then merges with a merge commit; it counts as landed and its file is graded exact.

title: Mervin board: cached, incremental, parallel checks, with timings
text:
Borg Mervin: fast and efficient (cached, incremental, parallel board)
Part of the borg Mervin push (see umbrella). The board reruns every stage from scratch each time. On 2026-10-13 it went over 30 PRs and 189 file merges, and it failed outright on a worktree without `node_modules` (`Cannot find module '@babel/parser'` from `src/lint.ts`), with no hint to run `bun install`.

- **Cache stages** by (main sha, PR head sha, the stages before it): if none of them moved, reuse the result. A new push reruns only that PR's stage and the ones after it.
- **Parallel where independent:** PRs that share no files don't affect each other, so merge them in parallel and serialize only where files overlap.
- **One install per wave** for `--check`, not per stage. Run only the touched apps' tests (as `scripts/ci-apps.ts` does).
- **Fail clearly:** a missing dependency says "run `bun install`" and stops early.
- **Print timings:** total wall time and per stage, so this issue can show its own before and after.

**Done when:** rerunning the board after one PR's push takes seconds, not a full pass, and the README states the time for a 30-PR board.

Mervin board: cached, incremental, parallel checks, with timings
Closes #1525

- Stages are cached (`.mervin/board-cache`) by main, the PR head and the state of each file it touches: a push reruns that PR's stage and only later stages sharing files with it.
- `--check` installs once and runs typecheck and touched apps' tests concurrently.
- Missing deps stop the board at the start with "run `bun install`".
- Prints per-stage and total wall time. 12 PRs / 59 file merges: 35.6s cold, 12.2s cached (docs/mervin.md).

Not done: merging disjoint PRs in parallel inside the merge loop; disjoint stages already skip via the cache, but a cold run is still sequential.

title: Mervin board: blame main for a conflict with main (#1522)
text:
Mervin board: a conflict with main gets blamed on an earlier stage's PR (#1489)
Seen on the 2026-10-13 board run (`bun scripts/mervin-board.ts`, 30 open PRs onto main 1450913c).

The board filed #1489's `apps/codesplitter/test/client.test.ts` as `mervin (after #1481)`, so the conflict looked like one that appears only once #1481 lands, and #1489 looked clean against main. GitHub says #1489 is `CONFLICTING` against main as it stands, and git agrees:

```
git merge-tree --write-tree --name-only origin/main origin/office/widget-1814
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in apps/codesplitter/test/client.test.ts
```

#1481's stage shows the same file as `mervin` with an empty `after`, so both PRs conflict with the same change on main. The `after` list seems to name only the earlier stages that touched the file and leaves out main.

**Fix:** when the file conflicts with main alone, say so (`after: main`, or a separate `conflictsWithMain` flag) and put it in the summary, so a wave plan never puts a PR GitHub can't merge into wave 1.

**Test:** a two-PR fixture where both PRs edit a line that main has also changed. The second PR's file must report main as the cause, not the first PR.

Mervin board: blame main for a conflict with main (#1522)
Closes #1522.

A file row now carries `main: true` when the PR's copy conflicts with main's own copy, whatever earlier stages did. The board prints `(conflicts with main)`, and `decide` holds such a PR (`conflicts with main on <files>`) so it never lands in wave 1.

Test: two PRs edit a line main also changed; both rows report main.

text:
Borg Mervin: knows all (one live board of every PR, its CI, stack, clashes and owner agent)
Part of the borg Mervin push (see umbrella). Mervin should hold one live picture of the repo, so nobody has to rerun the board by hand to find out where a round stands.

- **One live board:** update the stage of a PR whose head moved, or every stage when main moves (push/PR webhooks), instead of a one-off `mervin-board.ts` run.

text:
Mervin: merge-round blockers from the 10-13 round (umbrella #1526)
Blockers hit during the 10-13 merge round that Mervin could have prevented. Part of umbrella #1526.

1. **One red main test turned ~11 PRs red** (CSP test, fixed by #1536). Mervin should say "also failing on main" per PR, and rerun the failed jobs once the main fix merges. Related: #1531, #1534.
2. **Clean PRs went CONFLICTING after earlier merges** (#1517, #1507, #1489, #1467, #1493). Order the merges so cascade files land first or last (#1537), and warn before a merge that will conflict a waiting PR.

4. **mergeable is UNKNOWN right after each merge**, so a naive script skips good PRs. Mervin should poll and sequence merges instead.
5. **Merge method is easy to get wrong.** The brief said --merge for the round while the owner usually squashes; stacks need a merge commit but plain PRs want squash. Mervin should recommend a method per PR (stacked or not) and warn on a mismatch.

title: codeSplitter: watchdog Worker that rolls back to the last healthy version
text:
codeSplitter: hot backup and rollback, so it can host and redeploy its own code
Goal: codeSplitter's own code lives in codeSplitter, and agents edit, check, merge and redeploy the app that is hosting them (software-factory dogfood). That only works if a bad live edit can't take the host down with no way back.

## Slice 1: hot backup + rollback

- A tiny watchdog Worker, separate from the app, health-checks the primary on a cron (a cheap `/health`-style route) and calls the Workers API to roll back to the last known-good version when it fails N times in a row. Cloudflare Workers already keep versions, so no second full copy of the app is needed (no new spend beyond one cron Worker).
- Every deploy records its version id and is marked good only after the post-deploy health check passes; the watchdog rolls back to the newest good one.
- The rollback shows up as an event (repo activity, and an issue or fix task on the branch that shipped it, like self-healing CI #1015).
- Deploy keeps going through the existing DeployRunner; the watchdog never takes the deploy path itself, so a crashed app can't block its own rescue.

## Later slices (not this issue's first PR)

1. Self-hosted loop: codeSplitter's repo is a repo in codeSplitter; agents branch, run checks, merge vi
codeSplitter: watchdog Worker that rolls back to the last healthy version
Closes #1562 (slice 1: hot backup + rollback).

- `watchdog/`: a separate cron Worker. Each minute it calls `GET /api/health`; a version that answers while live is remembered as good, one that fails is forgotten. After 3 failures in a row it puts the newest good version on 100% via the Workers API. It never touches DeployRunner.

title: codeSplitter: log rollbacks with what shipped them, and TV view limits
text:
codeSplitter: hot backup and rollback, so it can host and redeploy its own code
Goal: codeSplitter's own code lives in codeSplitter, and agents edit, check, merge and redeploy the app that is hosting them (software-factory dogfood). That only works if a bad live edit can't take the host down with no way back.

## Slice 1: hot backup + rollback

- A tiny watchdog Worker, separate from the app, health-checks the primary on a cron (a cheap `/health`-style route) and calls the Workers API to roll back to the last known-good version when it fails N times in a row. Cloudflare Workers already keep versions, so no second full copy of the app is needed (no new spend beyond one cron Worker).
- Every deploy records its version id and is marked good only after the post-deploy health check passes; the watchdog rolls back to the newest good one.
- The rollback shows up as an event (repo activity, and an issue or fix task on the branch that shipped it, like self-healing CI #1015).
- Deploy keeps going through the existing DeployRunner; the watchdog never takes the deploy path itself, so a crashed app can't block its own rescue.
